steps.headingEn: Foundational Concepts: PMI, Exam Content Outline (ECO), and PMBOK® Guide 8
steps.bodyEn:
When starting your **PMP®** (*Project Management Professional*) exam preparation, you will encounter several specialized acronyms. Here are 5 core concepts to understand before diving into the knowledge domains:

- **PMI (*Project Management Institute*):** The international organization that establishes professional standards, administers exams, and awards the PMP credential globally.
- **ECO (*Exam Content Outline*):** The official document defining the exam structure, tested management tasks, and domain weightings. The current version is [!badge:violet:ECO 07/2026].
- **PMBOK® Guide 8th Edition (*Project Management Body of Knowledge*):** The foundational standard explaining project management principles, performance domains, and processes. While `ECO` defines the exam scope outline, `PMBOK® 8` serves as the foundational reference guide.
- **OCM (*Organizational Change Management*):** A structured set of activities that helps staff and end users adopt, adapt to, and integrate a new product into daily work rather than reverting to legacy habits.
- **ESG (*Environmental, Social, and Governance*):** A sustainability evaluation framework covering resource optimization, workplace safety, data security, and ethical governance.

> [!NOTE]
> **Software Project Perspective:** Project management goes far beyond building schedules (Gantt charts) and pushing tasks to finish on time. According to PMI standards, a project is only considered successful when its deliverables ==comply with regulatory requirements, are genuinely adopted by users, and generate sustainable business value==.

steps.headingEn: PMP Exam Structure (ECO 07/2026) and the Surge in Business Environment Weighting
steps.bodyEn:
The PMP exam consists of **180 questions** (175 scored questions + 5 randomly distributed *pretest* questions) over **240 minutes**, divided into three 60-question sections with two 10-minute breaks. The most notable change in [!badge:violet:ECO 07/2026] is that the **Business Environment** domain weighting more than tripled: jumping from `8%` to ==26% of the total exam score==.

Most questions describe a 3–5 line real-world scenario and ask: ==What should the project manager do FIRST / NEXT / BEST?== All 4 options often sound reasonable, but only **1 option follows PMI's standard decision-making sequence**.

steps.headingEn: The 3-Tier Architecture of PMBOK® Guide 8 and the PMP Mindmap
steps.bodyEn:
[!badge:amber:PMBOK 8] combines the value-driven mindset of the 7th edition with the clear process structure of the 6th edition into **3 tightly integrated tiers**:

- **Tier 1 — 6 Guiding Principles:** The ethical and decision-making compass (*Holistic View · Focus on Value · Embed Quality · Accountable Leader · Integrate Sustainability · Empowered Culture*).
- **Tier 2 — 5 Focus Areas:** The operational rhythm across every project (*Initiating · Planning · Executing · Monitoring & Controlling · Closing*) — executed across major phases in Waterfall, and iterated lightweight within every 2-week Sprint in Agile!
- **Tier 3 — 7 Performance Domains (40 processes):** Consolidates the former 10 knowledge areas into 7 intuitive domains: `Governance` (9), `Scope` (6), `Schedule` (3), `Finance` (4), `Stakeholders` (7), `Resources` (5), and `Risk` (6).

steps.headingEn: Integrated Scenario and Effective Study Strategy
steps.bodyEn:
Suppose you are a Tech Lead transitioning into the PM role for an E-Wallet project. During execution, the Central Bank issues a new regulation mandating biometric authentication (**Business Environment — Compliance**), causing confusion in the engineering team regarding work scope (**People**) and putting the release schedule at risk of delay (**Process**). A realistic PMP question often weaves all 3 domains into a single scenario to evaluate holistic orchestration capabilities.

> [!TIP]
> **4-Step Study Method on This Platform:**
> 1. Read each lesson section carefully to grasp the **core concepts and application context** before examining the illustrative examples.
> 2. Study the visual diagrams to understand ==cause-and-effect relationships across management components== rather than memorizing mechanically.
> 3. Complete the end-of-module Quiz to spot impulsive real-world habits that commonly cost points.
> 4. Cross-reference the supporting branches on **PMP Mindmap** and practice mock questions at a target pace of `~80 seconds/question`.

p00-q1.qEn: A Tech Lead with 8 years of experience is preparing for the PMP exam under ECO 07/2026. He plans to spend 95% of his time studying EVM formulas, CPM critical path calculations, and memorizing ITTOs, while skimming Business Environment in a single session because he thinks 'it is only 8% of the score'. What is the best advice for this plan?
choicesEn: Reasonable, because Process always accounts for 80% of calculation questions on the PMP exam.
A critical mistake: Under ECO 07/2026, Business Environment jumped from 8% to 26% (8 tasks), requiring solid mastery of Business Case, Benefits Realization, Compliance, OCM, and Sustainability.
Just skip the Predictive portion entirely because the new exam has shifted to 100% pure Scrum questions.
Focus on memorizing exact term definitions because 70% of the exam consists of fill-in-the-blank questions.
p00-q1.explainEn: Under ECO 07/2026, the 3 domain weightings are People 33% (8 tasks) · Process 41% (10 tasks) · Business Environment 26% (8 tasks — more than tripled from 8% in ECO 2021). Over 90% of the exam consists of applied situational questions spanning ~40% Predictive and ~60% Agile/Hybrid, not ITTO rote memorization.

p00-q2.qEn: When reading a 5-line situational question on the PMP exam screen ending with 'What should the project manager do FIRST?', what is the smartest strategy within 80 seconds?
choicesEn: Immediately pick the most decisive action option that resolves the issue fastest.
Choose the option to report immediately to the Project Sponsor to demonstrate transparency.
Read the closing question first to identify the keyword FIRST, locate the context (Predictive/Agile/Hybrid), and prioritize fact-checking / impact assessment before making a decision.
Look for the option containing the most complex PMBOK terminology and select it.
p00-q2.explainEn: On the PMP exam, keywords like FIRST / NEXT test the standard management reasoning sequence. All 4 options may be good actions, but the FIRST step is almost always verifying root facts, analyzing impact, or communicating directly to understand the root cause before taking action.

p00-q3.qEn: In the 7 Performance Domains (40 processes) structure of PMBOK® Guide 8th Edition (2025), which domain consolidates Integration Management, Manage Quality Assurance (Manage QA), and Plan Sourcing Strategy?
choicesEn: Finance Performance Domain
Governance Performance Domain
Resources Performance Domain
Stakeholders Performance Domain
p00-q3.explainEn: PMBOK 8 restructures processes into 7 Performance Domains. Domain #1 Governance (9 processes) serves as the overarching orchestration framework, consolidating the former Integration area along with Manage Quality Assurance and Plan Sourcing Strategy. When looking up contract details or quality tools in PMP Mindmap, review 'governance', 'procurement', and 'quality' together on the Book Map.

p00-q4.qEn: You want to open PMP Mindmap to view detailed diagrams on 'Business Case, NPV/IRR' and 'Regulatory Compliance'. Which edition should you select to see these topics in full?
choicesEn: The Core edition (ed=core), because all topics are contained within the 10 Core maps.
The Book edition (ed=book), because the 5 extended topics—'intro', 'business', 'value', 'governance', and 'procurement'—are covered in depth on the Book Map.
They are only viewable in Flashcard mode and do not exist on the Mindmap diagram.
Both editions have the exact same 14 topics.
p00-q4.explainEn: On PMP Mindmap, the Core edition condenses the 10 most essential practical maps (core.*), while the Book edition (ed=book) expands across all 14 topics including intro, business, value, governance, and procurement. The reference links in PMP Mastery already include the ed=book parameter for you.

p00-q5.qEn: According to PMBOK® Guide 8th Edition, the 5 Focus Areas (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) only exist in Predictive (Waterfall) projects and are completely eliminated in Agile.
p00-q5.explainEn: False! PMBOK 8 affirms that the 5 Focus Areas are present in EVERY development approach. The difference is that in Predictive they occur sequentially in large phases, whereas in Agile/Adaptive they repeat continuously at a smaller scale within each Release and each Sprint.

p00-c1.frontEn: What are the score weightings and task counts of the 3 domains in the PMP exam under ECO 07/2026?
p00-c1.backEn:
• People: 33% (8 tasks)
• Process: 41% (10 tasks)
• Business Environment: 26% (8 tasks — surged from the old 8%!)
Total: 180 questions / 240 minutes (~80 seconds/question), ~60% Agile & Hybrid contexts.

p00-c2.frontEn: Why did the Business Environment domain surge to 26% in ECO 07/2026?
p00-c2.backEn: PMI expects modern PMs not just to 'chase schedules' but to align projects with organizational strategy: validating the Business Case, Benefits Realization, Compliance, Organizational Change Management (OCM), Sustainability, and responsible AI adoption.

p00-c3.frontEn: What are the 7 Performance Domains (40 processes) of PMBOK® Guide 8th Edition?
p00-c3.backEn:
1. Governance (9 processes)
2. Scope (6 processes)
3. Schedule (3 processes)
4. Finance (4 processes — renamed from Cost)
5. Stakeholders (7 processes — includes Communications)
6. Resources (5 processes — includes Lead the Team)
7. Risk (6 processes)

p00-c4.frontEn: What is the strategy for reading PMP situational questions containing FIRST / NEXT / BEST?
p00-c4.backEn:
1. Read the final question sentence first (FIRST/NEXT or BEST).
2. Identify the context (Predictive, Agile, or Hybrid) and project phase.
3. For FIRST/NEXT: always prioritize verifying root data & assessing impact before acting.

p00-c5.frontEn: Which 5 topics on PMP Mindmap are only in the Book edition (ed=book) for full alignment with PMBOK 8?
p00-c5.backEn:
intro, business, value, governance, and procurement.
(The Core edition condenses 10 practical core.* maps, while the Book edition expands to all 14 topics).

P01.titleEn: Mindset Shift: From Real-World Habits to PMI Standard Principles
P01.summaryEn: Detailed breakdown of 6 real-world project management habits that lose points on the PMP exam, and how to apply the 6 core PMI action principles (Think Before Act · Limit Escalate · Do Not Remove · Follow the Process · Direct Communication · Confront Problems).
P01.mottoEn: Set aside ad-hoc firefighting reflexes · Apply a disciplined, ethical, root-cause-first PM mindset
P01.realWorldTrapEn: Jumping straight into fixing issues unilaterally for speed, escalating every blocker directly to the Sponsor, requesting a replacement whenever someone is slow, or quietly adding out-of-scope features to please a client.
P01.pmiMindsetShiftEn: In PMI's world, the PM is an autonomous, systematic leader: always verify root data before acting, resolve issues within your authority, hold private 1-on-1 conversations, coach instead of removing team members, and strictly honor established processes.

steps.headingEn: Real-World Improvisation vs. PMI Project Governance Standards
steps.bodyEn:
Before comparing scenarios, make sure you understand 4 governance roles and concepts that appear throughout the PMP exam:

- **Project Sponsor:** The senior executive who approves the budget, owns the business justification, and signs the Project Charter (equivalent to a VP of Product or Business Unit Director).
- **Project Charter:** The formal document approved by the Sponsor that authorizes the project's existence and grants the PM authority to apply organizational resources (often called the project's birth certificate).
- **Baseline:** The approved reference plan for `Scope`, `Schedule`, and `Cost` used as the benchmark to measure and control variances.
- **CCB (*Change Control Board*):** The authorized body responsible for reviewing, approving, or rejecting change requests that impact any `Baseline`.

In day-to-day operations across many engineering teams, managers often handle issues through quick improvisation: if a client messages asking for a small PDF export button, they tell a developer to spend 2 extra hours building it; if a junior developer writes buggy code, they stay up late rewriting it themselves (*Hero Coding*); if Infrastructure provisions servers slowly, they immediately complain to the Director (`Sponsor`) to apply pressure.

On the PMP exam, [!badge:rose:Common Pitfall] ==almost all emotional, process-bypassing reactions are wrong answers==. PMI standards are designed for large-scale, cross-functional projects—where unapproved code changes can compromise system security or violate contractual commitments.

> [!NOTE]
> **Understanding Servant Leadership Properly:** Being a PM under PMI standards is neither command-and-control micromanagement nor doing the team's technical work for them. The PM acts as a facilitator and enabler: ==protecting team focus, removing process impediments, and creating conditions for the team to thrive==.

> [!WARNING]
> **Spotting Trap Options:** Choices starting with *Immediately escalate*, *Ask HR to replace*, *Instruct the team to work overtime*, or *Pause all project work* are usually incorrect (except in emergencies involving human safety or legal violations).

steps.headingEn: PM Authority Boundaries and Valid Escalation Scenarios to the Sponsor
steps.bodyEn:
Suppose during a core banking system upgrade project, a developer mentions an unconfirmed rumor that the cloud authentication vendor is about to double its pricing. Choosing *"Report to the Sponsor to request additional budget"* right away is premature. The right reflex is: **review the signed vendor contract and assess the actual financial impact first**.

The PM is **permitted and expected** to escalate an issue to the `Project Sponsor` only in **3 situations that exceed the PM's authority**:

1. The change exceeds `Baseline` tolerances or requires releasing **Management Reserve** when the organization has no separate CCB.
2. Market or strategic shifts render the **Business Case no longer viable**, requiring the Sponsor to decide whether to pivot or terminate the project early (the PM cannot unilaterally cancel a project).
3. Cross-departmental or enterprise-level risks or conflicts extending beyond project boundaries.

> [!TIP]
> **Rule Before Escalating to the Sponsor:** ==Never pass an unanalyzed problem upward.== The PM must complete the impact analysis and bring **2–3 solution options with a specific recommendation** so the Sponsor can make an informed decision.

p01-q1.qEn: Midway through a Predictive project, a long-time client privately calls a Senior Developer asking for 'a tiny report export filter that takes only 3 hours to code and will not delay the schedule or cost extra'. The Senior Developer excitedly tells you (the PM) that he will build it for free this afternoon to maintain goodwill. What should you do?
choicesEn: Agree immediately since the change costs nothing and increases customer satisfaction.

Thank the developer for the goodwill, but instruct him to stop adding unapproved features, explain the risk of Gold Plating, and guide the request through impact assessment and Perform Integrated Change Control.
Send a warning email to the entire development team and ask the Functional Manager to discipline the Senior Developer.
Report immediately to the Project Sponsor so the Sponsor can call and reprimand the client.
p01-q1.explainEn: This is the classic real-world 'Gold Plating' trap! Under PMI standards (Follow the Process & Holistic View), no change is 'free and harmless'—even 3 hours of code introduces regression risk, consumes QA testing effort, and adds maintenance overhead. Any change touching the Scope Baseline must undergo impact analysis and formal change control.

p01-q2.qEn: During lunch, you overhear an analyst mention that a key hardware vendor is about to discontinue the chip model your project uses, threatening a 2-month schedule delay. What should you do FIRST?
choicesEn: Immediately terminate the current contract and sign an emergency contract with an alternative vendor.
Immediately report to the Project Sponsor requesting a 2-month extension to the project completion milestone.
Verify the accuracy of the information with the vendor point of contact and work with the team to assess the actual impact on the project.
Submit a Change Request to the CCB right away to revise the Schedule Baseline.
p01-q2.explainEn: Principle #1 (Think Before Act): Never take drastic action or escalate based on unverified hallway rumors! The FIRST step is always to verify facts at the source and analyze the actual degree of impact.

p01-q3.qEn: A new team member joined the project 3 weeks ago but consistently misses task estimates and fails to follow internal coding standards. Which response reflects the proper PMI PM mindset?
choicesEn: Ask the Functional Manager to immediately replace the person with a more senior engineer to protect the schedule.
Meet privately 1-on-1 with the team member to uncover the root cause, then arrange targeted training or pairing/mentoring with a senior team member.
Take away all complex tasks from that person and assign them to the Tech Lead as overtime work.
Publicly criticize the team member during the weekly status meeting to set an example.
p01-q3.explainEn: Combines two core PMI principles: Direct Communication (private 1-on-1 discussion to diagnose the root cause) and Do Not Remove (training, coaching, and pairing rather than firing or public shaming).

p01-q4.qEn: In which of the following scenarios is it APPROPRIATE under PMI standards for the Project Manager to escalate an issue to the Project Sponsor?
choicesEn: Two lead engineers disagree on which database architecture to select.
A stakeholder complains that the weekly status report is too long and hard to read.
A newly enacted law requires a 35% budget increase, exhausting the entire Contingency Reserve and exceeding the PM's approval authority.
A team member arrives late to the Daily Standup twice in one week.
p01-q4.explainEn: Limit Escalate rule: Internal technical disagreements, communication formatting, and meeting discipline fall squarely within the PM's and team's authority. Only when an event breaches the Baseline / Contingency Reserve and impacts strategic funding (Management Reserve / Business Case) does the PM submit analyzed options to the Sponsor/CCB.

p01-q5.qEn: Two key team members have been arguing intensely for days over the automated testing solution, creating tension across the team and stalling progress. How should the PM approach this?
choicesEn: Ignore it for now because it is a technical matter and let the engineers resolve it over time (Withdraw).
Use positional authority to force both to adopt the more senior engineer's approach to save time (Force).

Facilitate a direct session with both members, reference the Ground Rules in the Team Charter, and guide an objective data-driven pros/cons analysis to find the optimal solution (Collaborate / Problem Solve).
Move the two individuals onto separate projects so they no longer interact.
p01-q5.explainEn: Confront Problems & Direct Communication: A PM never avoids conflict that harms the project. PMI's #1 preferred conflict resolution technique is always Collaborate / Problem Solve (collaborating based on objective facts and the Team Charter).

p01-q6.qEn: When escalating an out-of-authority issue to the Project Sponsor, the PM should immediately report the raw problem status and wait for the Sponsor to come up with resolution options.
p01-q6.explainEn: False! Even when escalation to the Sponsor is warranted, a PMI-aligned PM must complete the impact analysis first and bring well-structured options along with a clear recommendation.

p01-c1.frontEn: What are the 6 PMI standard situational principles that help eliminate trap choices on the PMP exam?
p01-c1.backEn:
1. Think Before Act (Analyze & verify before acting)
2. Limit Escalate (Do not push in-authority issues up to the Sponsor)
3. Do Not Remove (Coach/pair instead of firing team members)
4. Follow the Process (Respect Change Control & role authority)
5. Direct Communication (Hold private 1-on-1 conversations first)
6. Confront Problems (Address early via Collaborate/Problem Solve)

p01-c2.frontEn: Why is quietly adding a small 'free' feature to please a client (Gold Plating) always a WRONG answer in PMP?
p01-c2.backEn: Because every line of code or item added outside the Scope Baseline consumes testing effort, introduces regression risk, increases maintenance cost, and bypasses formal value evaluation through Change Control.

p01-c3.frontEn: When a question asks 'What should the PM do FIRST?' right after hearing negative news or a new issue, what is the first step?
p01-c3.backEn: Pause to verify the facts at the source (Verify/Investigate), review the current plans/documents, and assess impact (Assess impact) with the team—never rush to change a Baseline or notify the Sponsor.

p01-c4.frontEn: When IS the Project Manager ALLOWED to escalate an issue to the Project Sponsor?
p01-c4.backEn:
When the issue exceeds the PM's Project Charter authority:
• Exceeds Baseline tolerances / requires Management Reserve (when no separate CCB exists)
• Business Case loses viability (requiring pivot or early closure)
• Strategic risks impacting program or enterprise level.
(Always bring impact analysis & a recommendation!).

p01-c5.frontEn: When a team member underperforms or lacks skills, what is the standard PMI reflex?
p01-c5.backEn: Have a private 1-on-1 conversation (Direct & Private) to identify the root cause, then support with Training, Coaching, or Pairing/Mentoring. Never fire or publicly criticize.

p01-c6.frontEn: Which conflict resolution technique does PMI always prioritize highest when time and willingness to cooperate exist?
p01-c6.backEn: Collaborate / Problem Solve: direct dialogue examining objective data to achieve a sustainable Win-Win outcome rather than avoiding (Withdraw) or imposing (Force).

P02.titleEn: Holistic View, Focus on Value & Sustainability (PMBOK® 8 Principles #1 · #2 · #5)
P02.summaryEn: Master 3 strategic principles of PMBOK® 8 (Standard §3.3, §3.4, §3.7): evaluating systemic ripple effects (Holistic View), clearly distinguishing Output ≠ Outcome ≠ Benefits alongside MVP vs MMF (Focus on Value), and embedding ESG sustainability standards across both project delivery and product lifecycle (Sustainability).
P02.mottoEn: Delivering on plan without creating value—or causing long-term harm—is still a failed project
P02.realWorldTrapEn: Focusing solely on completing 100% of WBS work packages regardless of market shifts ('delivering Outputs means my job is done'), or picking the cheapest materials to optimize short-term budget while causing pollution and tripling operational costs.
P02.pmiMindsetShiftEn: A PM must view the project as a living system tied to the Business Case: changing one variable shifts every constraint; slice delivery to realize early value (MVP/MMF); recommend early closure if business viability vanishes; and embed sustainability from day one.

steps.headingEn: The Project Value Chain: Distinguishing Output, Outcome, and Benefits
steps.bodyEn:
A common misconception among technical teams is that delivering 100% of specified features on time and within budget guarantees project success. From the [!badge:amber:PMBOK 8] perspective, a project is still considered a failure if the deliverables are not adopted by users or fail to generate business value for the organization.

To master **Principle #2 — Focus on Value** (`PMBOK 8 §3.4`), distinguish these 3 value tiers using an **Online Medical Appointment Booking App** project example:

- **Output / Deliverable:** The tested iOS/Android app and booking APIs delivered on schedule. This is only the technical output—it does not automatically create business value.
- **Outcome:** 70% of patients shift from queuing in person for paper tickets to booking appointments via the mobile app.
- **Benefits:** Average wait time drops from 90 minutes to 10 minutes, hospital service capacity increases by 25%, and net annual revenue grows by 8 billion VND/year (reflected in financial metrics like positive **NPV** — *Net Present Value* and **ROI** — *Return on Investment*).

steps.headingEn: Comparing Two Early-Delivery Strategies: MVP vs. MMF
steps.bodyEn:
When needing to bring a product to market early to reduce the risk of long-term investment without feedback, the PMP exam frequently tests your ability to distinguish **MVP** from **MMF**:

| Full Term | Core Nature | Primary Goal | Real-World Example in a Food Delivery App |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **MVP** *(Minimum Viable Product)* | **Minimal prototype built to validate a hypothesis** | ==Validate market demand== at the lowest cost before scaling investment. | Quickly launch a simple webpage allowing 5 lunch items to be ordered in 1 office building for 2 weeks to measure real order rates. |
| **MMF** *(Minimum Marketable Feature)* | **Smallest feature set with standalone commercial value** | ==Generate revenue or solve 1 complete user need== immediately upon release. | Fully release a stable "One-Tap Apple Pay Checkout" feature to boost conversion rates right away. |

> [!TIP]
> **Exam Clues to Distinguish Them:** When the scenario emphasizes *test a hypothesis, validate customer interest, gather early feedback under high uncertainty* → choose **MVP**. When the scenario emphasizes *deliver immediate business value, generate early revenue, usable feature set* → choose **MMF**.

steps.headingEn: Systems Thinking (Holistic View) and Sustainability (ESG)
steps.bodyEn:
The next two paired principles in [!badge:amber:PMBOK 8] are **Principle #1 — Adopt a Holistic View** (`§3.3`) and **Principle #5 — Integrate Sustainability** (`§3.7`):

- **Holistic View:** A project operates as an interconnected system—changing one variable (for example, cutting 2 weeks of testing to meet a launch date) creates immediate ripple effects on Quality, Security Risk, Brand Reputation, and Post-Launch Maintenance Cost. Every change therefore requires a ==multi-dimensional Holistic Impact Assessment== before deciding.
- **Integrate Sustainability (ESG):** Directly aligned with the 26% Business Environment weighting, the PM must evaluate environmental, human, and full life-cycle operational impacts across two dimensions:

steps.headingEn: Handling Lost Business Viability and Avoiding the Sunk Cost Trap
steps.bodyEn:
Consider a common exam scenario: A company has spent **$800,000 (80% of its budget)** over 9 months building an internal payment gateway. Suddenly, a competitor releases a free international standard solution that integrates in 1 day, leaving the company's product uncompetitive even with another $200,000 invested. A team member suggests finishing it anyway because 80% of the budget is already spent.

> [!WARNING]
> **Avoid the Sunk Cost Fallacy:** The $800,000 already spent is an unrecoverable past cost; continuing to fund a project that has lost its `Outcome / Benefits` only compounds the loss. PMI standard action: ==Re-evaluate the Business Case & Benefits Management Plan → Present transparent data to the Project Sponsor to consider pivoting or conducting a controlled early project closure==.

p02-q1.qEn: An internal payment gateway project is 75% complete, on schedule, and within budget. Suddenly, the Central Bank releases a new free interoperability standard that eliminates the proprietary solution's competitive advantage, and ongoing operating costs will exceed projected revenue. What should the PM do NEXT?
choicesEn: Have the team accelerate the remaining 25% so the project can be recorded as delivered on time and on budget.
Work with stakeholders to re-evaluate the Business Case & Benefits Management Plan, then present the data and options (pivoting objectives or early closure) to the Project Sponsor.
Withhold the market news to avoid hurting developer morale.
Unilaterally disband the project team that same day to save the remaining 25% of the budget.
p02-q1.explainEn: Under Principle #2 (Focus on Value): The 75% already spent is a Sunk Cost. Continuing to burn the remaining 25% on a product that no longer yields positive Outcomes/Benefits wastes organizational resources. However, the PM does not have authority to cancel a project unilaterally, and must instead reassess the Business Case and present recommendations to the Sponsor.

p02-q2.qEn: A startup is uncertain whether enterprise customers are willing to pay for an 'Automated Contract Summarization Assistant' feature. They want to build the leanest possible test version in 2 weeks to measure actual sign-up click rates and gather feedback before making a major investment. What is this artifact accurately called?
choicesEn: Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)
Minimum Viable Product (MVP)
Minimum Marketable Feature (MMF)
Gold Plating Prototype
p02-q2.explainEn: The key clues are 'uncertain market hypothesis → build the leanest version to validate and learn from real feedback': this is the exact definition of an MVP (Minimum Viable Product). Once the hypothesis is proven and complete feature slices need to be released commercially, you use MMF.

p02-q3.qEn: When evaluating bids for a new data center, Contractor A quotes 12% lower, leaving a budget surplus, but their cooling units consume twice the electricity and use refrigerants scheduled for restriction under environmental regulations in 3 years. Contractor B's quote fits within the baseline budget and meets long-term energy efficiency standards. Under PMBOK 8 Principle #5, what should the PM recommend?
choicesEn: Select Contractor A because the PM's responsibility ends on the day of handover sign-off, and electricity costs belong to Operations.
Evaluate Life-cycle Costing and sustainability compliance risks (Sustainability BY the product), and recommend selecting Contractor B.
Select Contractor A and cut safety testing steps to save even more money.
Split the contract between both contractors to install mixed equipment in the same server room.
p02-q3.explainEn: PMBOK 8's new Principle #5 (Integrate Sustainability Within All Project Areas) combined with Holistic View requires the PM to consider economic, environmental, and social impacts across the entire product life cycle (Total Cost of Ownership / Life-cycle Cost), rather than locally optimizing short-term capex at the expense of Operations.

p02-q4.qEn: The Marketing Director asks to pull the app launch date forward by 3 weeks to catch a trade expo, while insisting that 100% of feature scope must remain unchanged. Which PM response reflects Principle #1 (Adopt a Holistic View)?
choicesEn: Immediately update the Schedule Baseline to shorten it by 3 weeks as requested by the Marketing Director.
Conduct a comprehensive analysis of the ripple effects of schedule compression on Cost, Resources, system defect Risk, QA Quality, and Operations readiness before presenting trade-off options.
Mandate that the entire development team work 14 hours a day for 1 consecutive month.
Flatly refuse without evaluating the business value of the trade expo.
p02-q4.explainEn: Adopt a Holistic View: Compressing Schedule while holding Scope fixed inevitably impacts Finance (Crashing), Risk/Rework (Fast-tracking), Quality, and Resource well-being. Meanwhile, the expo may hold substantial Value, so do not refuse blindly—analyze holistic trade-off options first.

p02-q5.qEn: A project that delivers 100% of technical Deliverables (Outputs) according to specifications, on time, and within budget is always considered fully successful by PMI, even if customers never use the product and no business benefits are realized.
p02-q5.explainEn: False! Under PMBOK 8 (§3.4 Focus on Value), Deliverables (Outputs) are merely the means. True project success is measured by realizing the intended Outcomes and strategic Benefits defined in the Business Case & Benefits Management Plan.

p02-c1.frontEn: How do the 3 tiers Output · Outcome · Benefits differ under PMBOK 8 Principle #2 (Focus on Value)?
p02-c1.backEn:
• Output (Deliverable): The product/artifact produced (e.g., a new CRM software).
• Outcome: The behavioral or capability shift upon adoption (e.g., sales reps look up customer history 3x faster).
• Benefits: Quantifiable/strategic value gained (e.g., +18% deal close rate, positive NPV).

p02-c2.frontEn: What is the deciding difference between an MVP (Minimum Viable Product) and an MMF (Minimum Marketable Feature)?
p02-c2.backEn:
• MVP: Aims to LEARN & VALIDATE high-risk hypotheses at minimum cost/time.
• MMF: Aims to DELIVER REAL VALUE / REVENUE from the smallest complete feature set users will adopt or pay for.

p02-c3.frontEn: What does PMBOK 8 Principle #1 (Adopt a Holistic View) require the PM to do when one project variable changes?
p02-c3.backEn: Always assess ripple effects across the entire system: Scope ↔ Schedule ↔ Finance ↔ Quality ↔ Resources ↔ Risk, plus alignment with the external environment and Operations before deciding.

p02-c4.frontEn: What are the two dimensions of PMBOK 8's new Principle #5 'Integrate Sustainability Within All Project Areas' (§3.7)?
p02-c4.backEn:
1. Sustainability OF the project: Sustainable delivery practices (green procurement, labor ethics, team safety & well-being).
2. Sustainability BY the product: Sustainability across the product's operational and disposal life cycle post-closure (ESG, resource efficiency, Life-cycle Cost).

p02-c5.frontEn: If a project is 80% complete but external shifts render the Business Case no longer valuable, what must the PM do?
p02-c5.backEn: Do not fall into the Sunk Cost trap! Re-evaluate the Business Case & Benefits Management Plan, then transparently report findings with recommendations to the Project Sponsor to consider pivoting or controlled early termination.

P03.titleEn: Embed Quality, Accountable Leader & Empowered Culture (Principles #3 · #4 · #6)
P03.summaryEn: Master the three people and quality principles of PMBOK® 8 (Standard §3.5, §3.6, §3.8): embedding quality into processes rather than relying on late-stage defect inspection (Embed Quality), leading with integrity and reporting bad news early (Accountable Leader), and cultivating a psychologically safe culture for self-organizing teams (Empowered Culture).
P03.mottoEn: Quality is non-negotiable · Report bad news early · Teams thrive through trust and empowerment
P03.realWorldTrapEn: Cutting back on testing (QC) under schedule pressure, hiding schedule slippage out of fear of executive reprimand while hoping the team catches up, or estimating work yourself and forcing the team to commit to the PM's numbers.
P03.pmiMindsetShiftEn: Preventing defects in the process (Prevention) is always cheaper than fixing external failures; Low Grade can be acceptable, but Low Quality is strictly forbidden; accountable leaders must be completely honest with data and empower the people doing the work to estimate it.

steps.headingEn: Three Core Concepts: Psychological Safety, Reporting Transparency, and Quality vs. Grade
steps.bodyEn:
In projects under intense schedule pressure, weekly status reports often keep showing green right up until the handover date, when critical defects and severe delays suddenly surface. In project management, hiding poor actual performance behind a reassuring report is commonly called a **"Watermelon Status Report"** (*green on the outside, red on the inside*).

To prevent this trap and build sustainable teams, [!badge:amber:PMBOK 8] emphasizes three core concepts:

- **Psychological Safety:** A high-trust work environment where a team member who accidentally introduces a configuration error or uncovers an architectural risk ==feels safe speaking up immediately== without fear of criticism, punishment, or personal blame.
- **Servant Leadership:** A leadership style focused on removing impediments, providing the right tools, and shielding the team from unnecessary pressure so they can focus on delivering value.
- **Quality vs. Grade:** You must distinguish these two concepts sharply in practice and on the PMP exam. **Quality** is the degree to which a product fulfills agreed requirements, operates reliably, and has minimal defects; **Grade** is the category or richness of features and technical bells and whistles. A note-taking app with basic functionality (**Low Grade**) that runs reliably without data loss (**High Quality**) is acceptable; conversely, a feature-rich app (**High Grade**) plagued by frequent crashes and critical bugs (**Low Quality**) is ==non-compliant and completely unacceptable==.

steps.headingEn: Principle #3 — Embed Quality and Cost of Quality (CoQ)
steps.bodyEn:
Many project teams fall into the habit of coding quickly and deferring all defect discovery to end-of-cycle testing. The **Cost of Quality (CoQ)** rule demonstrates that the later a defect is detected, the more exponentially expensive it becomes to fix (1 cost unit during design → 10 units during coding → 100 units when an incident hits production).

```visual

title: "Ba Nguyên tắc Trọng tâm về Quản lý Chất lượng (PMBOK® 8)"
subtitle: "Phòng ngừa lỗi trong quy trình luôn hiệu quả hơn kiểm tra sửa lỗi ở cuối nguồn"
items:
  - keyword: "Quality vs Grade"
    role: "Độ chính xác cam kết vs Mức độ tính năng"
    tone: "amber"
    summary: "Khi thiếu ngân sách hoặc gấp tiến độ, có thể trình duyệt hạ **Grade** (giảm bớt tính năng phụ), nhưng **TUYỆT ĐỐI KHÔNG** cắt bớt kiểm thử hay hạ chuẩn **Quality**."
    bullets:
      - "Các phương án gợi ý 'Skip integration testing to meet the deadline' luôn là phương án sai."
  - keyword: "Cost of Conformance"
    role: "Chi phí Tuân thủ (Đầu tư phòng ngừa)"
    tone: "emerald"
    summary: "Chi phí bỏ ra để **ngăn ngừa lỗi từ đầu** (Prevention: đào tạo, quy chuẩn code, CI/CD linter, DoD) và **kiểm tra sớm** (Appraisal: peer review, automated test)."
    bullets:
      - "Luôn thấp hơn nhiều lần so với Cost of Nonconformance (Rework, bảo hành, phạt hợp đồng, mất uy tín)."
  - keyword: "Built-in Quality"
    role: "Tích hợp chất lượng vào quy trình"
    tone: "sky"
    summary: "Chất lượng thuộc trách nhiệm chung của **cả đội dự án ở từng bước thực thi**, không phải việc riêng của bộ phận QA/Tester ở cuối Sprint."
```

steps.headingEn: Principle #4 — Accountable Leader and the PMI Code of Ethics
steps.bodyEn:
Being an **Accountable Leader** requires honest stewardship grounded in the **4 core values of the PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct**: *Responsibility · Respect · Fairness · Honesty*.

- **Transparency in reporting metrics:** If actual schedule performance is 20% behind, even if senior management hints at adjusting the status color to keep the client calm, PMI's mandatory standard is to ==refuse to falsify metrics and report the true status honestly alongside root-cause analysis and a corrective action plan==.
- **Avoiding Conflicts of Interest:** Do not accept high-value gifts from vendors; if you discover that a relative's company is bidding on a contract, **disclose it transparently right away** and recuse yourself from the evaluation committee.
- **Protecting Intellectual Property & Confidential Data:** Do not bring proprietary source code or documents from a previous organization into a new project, and do not paste unredacted customer data into public AI tools.

> [!WARNING]
> **Note on cross-border ethics scenarios:** The exam may present a scenario where an unofficial payment is considered customary locally to expedite paperwork. Always distinguish between *a legal administrative fee backed by an official government receipt* (permitted) and *an unlawful bribe* (strictly prohibited under PMI standards).

steps.headingEn: Principle #6 — Empowered Culture and Servant Leadership
steps.bodyEn:
When teams are given true **Empowerment** paired with clear goals, their performance and decision-making speed far outperform micromanagement:

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Quản lý Vi mô Áp đặt vs Văn hoá Trao quyền & An toàn Tâm lý"
subtitle: "Người trực tiếp thực thi kỹ thuật là người nắm rõ nhất giải pháp và mức độ nỗ lực cần thiết"
left:
  badge: "MICROMANAGEMENT (KHÔNG PHÙ HỢP)"
  title: "Áp đặt · Truy tìm lỗi cá nhân · Giấu vấn đề"
  tone: "rose"
  bullets:
    - "PM tự ước lượng thời gian từng task rồi ép thành viên ký cam kết thực hiện theo."
    - "Khi hệ thống gặp sự cố Production, tổ chức họp chỉ trích cá nhân để răn đe."
    - "PM tự soạn nội quy làm việc áp đặt từ trên xuống cho toàn đội."
right:
  badge: "EMPOWERED CULTURE (CHUẨN PMI)"
  title: "Tự tổ chức · Học từ sự cố · Đồng thuận"
  tone: "emerald"
  bullets:
    - "Để chính các thành viên chuyên môn tự ước lượng nỗ lực và chủ động nhận đầu việc."
    - "Tổ chức Blameless Postmortem / Retrospective: tìm lỗ hổng quy trình thay vì đổ lỗi cá nhân."
    - "Cả đội cùng thảo luận và đồng kiến tạo bản quy ước làm việc chung (Team Charter)."
```

> [!TIP]
> **General rule for People & Quality exam questions:** When a team faces recurring defects, the right answer is almost always ==improving preventive processes (Built-in Quality / QA) combined with training in a psychologically safe environment==—never cutting testing or punishing individuals.

p03-q1.qEn: A project developing a handheld medical device is at risk of exceeding its budget by 15%. In an urgent meeting, a team member proposes two ways to save money: (Option 1) Cut 50% of the sensor accuracy tests; (Option 2) Keep all safety and accuracy testing intact, but drop the decorative color touchscreen and revert to a standard monochrome display if the customer agrees. According to PMBOK 8 Principle #3, what should the PM do?
choicesEn: Choose Option 1 because users prefer an attractive color display over behind-the-scenes testing.
Immediately reject Option 1 (because compromising Quality is unacceptable) and collaborate with the customer/CCB to evaluate Option 2 (reducing secondary Grade/Scope while preserving core Quality).
Apply both Option 1 and Option 2 without notifying the customer.
Ask team members to pay out of pocket for components to keep both the color screen and all tests.
p03-q1.explainEn: Key distinction in PMBOK 8 §3.5: Low Grade (a durable, compliant monochrome screen with fewer decorative features) can be a valid design trade-off if approved through Change Control; however, Low Quality (cutting tests that jeopardize medical sensor accuracy) is strictly FORBIDDEN.

p03-q2.qEn: Before a phase-gate review meeting with the customer, your department director (your direct manager) messages you privately: 'The actual CPI is 0.82, but let's report it as 0.98 this week so the client doesn't escalate—we'll figure out how to recover next month.' As an Accountable Leader under PMI standards, what should you do?
choicesEn: Follow the department director's instruction because senior management holds ultimate accountability to the company.
Professionally refuse to falsify the data, explain your obligation to honesty, and report the true CPI of 0.82 along with root-cause analysis and a corrective action plan.
Cancel the customer meeting indefinitely to avoid submitting any report.
Send a blank status report with no financial figures at all.
p03-q2.explainEn: Principle #4 (Be an Accountable Leader) and the Honesty value in the PMI Code of Ethics: falsifying reports is a serious ethical violation. The PM must professionally refuse the improper request and present the objective truth accompanied by remediation options.

p03-q3.qEn: At the start of a new Agile project, a Project Manager transitioning from a traditional environment personally creates a detailed hour-by-hour estimate for every User Story and hands it to the Developers to execute. As a result, the team stays silent, lacks commitment, and repeatedly misses Sprint targets. What is the PM's core mistake?
choicesEn: The PM's estimates were not granular enough down to the minute.
The PM violated Principle #6 (Build an Empowered Culture) by not letting the Developers who actually do the work estimate effort and self-organize their Sprint plan.
The PM forgot to impose financial penalties on team members who worked slower than the estimate.
Estimation is never permitted for any work in Agile.
p03-q3.explainEn: Under Principle #6 (Empowered Culture) and Scrum, the people doing the work (Developers) must estimate the effort themselves (e.g., via Planning Poker) and own the Sprint execution plan. Top-down imposition destroys commitment and estimation accuracy.

p03-q4.qEn: The project team has just completed internal testing for a software module, confirming the product meets 100% of technical specifications (Verified Deliverable). However, over the past two weeks the team noticed that the test-environment handoff process between Dev and QA is chaotic and wastes many hours of waiting. Reviewing and optimizing this collaboration process belongs to which area?
choicesEn: Validate Scope
Control Quality (QC)
Manage Quality / Quality Assurance (QA) combined with process improvement in a Retrospective / Lessons Learned
Close Project
p03-q4.explainEn: Control Quality (QC) inspects the correctness of a specific PRODUCT; Validate Scope handles formal acceptance with the CUSTOMER; evaluating and improving the WORK PROCESS to prevent waste and defects belongs to Manage Quality / QA (under PMBOK 8 Governance) and continuous improvement.

p03-q5.qEn: During a Sprint Retrospective, a junior developer nervously admits they ran the wrong configuration script and brought down the Staging environment for 4 hours. Which response from the PM / Scrum Master reinforces Psychological Safety and long-term quality?
choicesEn: Issue a formal written warning to the developer and permanently revoke their system access.
Thank them for their honesty, maintain a blameless mindset, and facilitate the team in adding automated checks or two-step confirmation so no one can make that mistake again.
Require the developer to work over the weekend alone to make up for the mistake.
Report the developer's name directly to the Project Sponsor.
p03-q5.explainEn: This seamlessly integrates all three principles: #3 (Prevention over Inspection—adding automated safeguards to the process), #4 (Accountable Leader), and #6 (Empowered Culture—psychological safety that turns errors into system improvements rather than individual punishment).

p03-c1.frontEn: How do you distinguish 'Quality' and 'Grade' on the PMP exam?
p03-c1.backEn:
• Quality: The degree to which a deliverable meets stated requirements (defect-free, compliant). Low Quality is NEVER acceptable!
• Grade: Category/richness of features or technical specs. Low Grade with High Quality (fewer extras, works flawlessly) is completely VALID.

p03-c2.frontEn: Sharply distinguish 3 concepts: Manage Quality (QA) · Control Quality (QC) · Validate Scope.
p03-c2.backEn:
• Manage Quality (QA): Auditing & improving PROCESSES to prevent defects.
• Control Quality (QC): Inspecting the internal PRODUCT → produces Verified Deliverables.
• Validate Scope: Customer/Sponsor formal acceptance review → produces Accepted Deliverables.

p03-c3.frontEn: What do 'Cost of Quality (CoQ)' and 'Prevention over Inspection' mean in PMBOK 8 Principle #3?
p03-c3.backEn: Investing in defect prevention within the process (training, standardization, automated tests — Cost of Conformance) is always far cheaper than internal rework and especially defects reaching the customer (External Failure — Cost of Nonconformance).

p03-c4.frontEn: When a manager or client pressures you to sugarcoat schedule/cost reports or ignore a safety risk, what does an Accountable Leader do?
p03-c4.backEn: Strictly uphold the PMI Code of Ethics (Honesty & Responsibility): refuse to falsify data, report bad news EARLY and TRANSPARENTLY along with root-cause analysis and corrective options.

p03-c5.frontEn: What are the 3 pillars for building an 'Empowered Culture' (PMBOK 8 Principle #6) in a project team?
p03-c5.backEn:
1. Let the people doing the work estimate and self-assign tasks.
2. Foster Psychological Safety & Blameless Learning (fix processes rather than blaming people).
3. Co-create a Team Charter / Ground Rules with team consensus.

P04.titleEn: Selecting a Development Approach: Predictive, Iterative, Incremental, Agile & Hybrid
P04.summaryEn: Master the framework for diagnosing and selecting a development approach under PMBOK® 8 (Standard §4.2–4.3) and the Stacey Matrix: sharply distinguish Iterative (repeating prototypes to get it RIGHT) from Incremental (slicing to deliver FAST), how Agile combines both in short Timeboxes, and how the 5 Focus Areas operate across every life cycle.
P04.mottoEn: There is no one-size-fits-all method — Requirements and Technical Uncertainty dictate the path
P04.realWorldTrapEn: Picking 'Agile' reflexively in every question regardless of context, or treating Iterative and Incremental as identical and losing points on lifecycle questions tied to business goals.
P04.pmiMindsetShiftEn: Choose the approach based on three factors: requirements clarity, technical stability, and early delivery needs—pick Iterative to validate correctness through prototype feedback, Incremental to deliver usable slices early, Agile when both dimensions are volatile, and Hybrid when components have differing characteristics.

steps.headingEn: Five Project Development Approaches in PMBOK® 8 (Predictive, Iterative, Incremental, Agile, Hybrid)
steps.bodyEn:
When building a new product or system, no single management approach fits every context. In [!badge:amber:PMBOK 8] (`Standard §4.2`), PMI arranges approaches along a **Development Spectrum** guided by the **Stacey Matrix**: uncertainty of **Requirements (What)** × uncertainty of **Technology/Implementation (How)**, combined with **Cost of Change**.

Using the same context of building an e-commerce platform and payment infrastructure, we can distinguish the 5 approaches:

1. **Predictive (*Waterfall — Sequential & Plan-Driven*):** Constructing a physical server room or a tax-filing portal governed by 100% locked statutory regulations. Design is finalized upfront before sequential execution, ==delivering the complete package once at the end of the project== because tearing down and rebuilding is prohibitively expensive.
2. **Iterative (*Refinement Cycles — Optimizing CORRECTNESS*):** Designing a complex stock-trading interface where the client does not yet know which layout works best. The team builds a wireframe → color mockup → interactive prototype across multiple feedback rounds until the design is spot-on, then delivers the final release.
3. **Incremental (*Part-by-Part Growth — Optimizing DELIVERY SPEED*):** The overall vision is clear, but the business needs to launch and generate revenue early: Month 1 releases 100% of Cart + Cash-on-Delivery (immediately usable); Month 2 adds E-wallets; Month 3 adds Loyalty Points.
4. **Agile / Adaptive (*Iterative + Incremental*):** Slicing the project into fixed short cycles of **1–4 weeks (Sprint / Timebox)**—each Sprint both gathers feedback to clarify evolving requirements and ships a working increment.
5. **Hybrid (*Intentional Blending*):** A Smart EV Charging Station project—the civil foundation and charger installation stream runs **Predictive** (you cannot dig up a street every 2 weeks!), while the mobile station-finder app runs **Agile Scrum**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Analogy to distinguish Iterative vs. Incremental:** Think of painting a portrait:
> - **Iterative:** Sketch the full composition in pencil → block in rough colors → refine fine details. Each pass makes the painting *more accurate*, but it is only ready for use at the final pass.
> - **Incremental:** Complete 100% of the face → complete the background → complete secondary details. Each finished slice delivers *complete usable value for that portion right away*.

steps.headingEn: The Inverted Triangle of Constraints and 4 Common Hybrid Models
steps.bodyEn:
The fundamental shift between traditional and adaptive thinking lies in the **Inverted Triangle of Constraints**:

- In **Predictive**, ==`Scope` is pinned fixed at the top of the triangle==; from that scope, the PM derives how many months (`Schedule`) and how much money (`Finance`) are needed.
- In **Agile**, the organization **pins Time (`2-week Sprints`) and Cost (`a stable 7-person team`) fixed**, then adjusts **Scope (`Product Backlog`)** so that ==the highest-business-value features are always delivered first==!

In practice and on the [!badge:violet:ECO 07/2026], you will encounter 4 common **Hybrid** patterns: (1) *Agile first, Predictive second* (prototyping an AI model with Agile, then rolling it out across 200 branches via Waterfall); (2) *Predictive first, Agile second*; (3) *Parallel simultaneous streams* (hardware and software teams syncing at shared integration milestones); and (4) *A predominantly Predictive framework embedding a small Agile component*.

steps.bodyEn:

steps.headingEn: Tailoring Principles When Transitioning to Agile
steps.bodyEn:
**Tailoring** means the PM proactively selects and adapts processes to fit organizational culture, team capability, and product complexity—rather than rigidly applying a textbook template.

> [!TIP]
> **Handling organizational transformation questions on the exam:** If a scenario describes a traditional organization (such as a long-established bank used to strict governance) wanting to adopt Agile, the right answer is **never** *"Immediately delete all documentation and force a 100% Scrum switch next Monday."* The PMI-aligned approach is to ==implement a transitional Hybrid model, start with a Pilot project, and provide step-by-step training and Coaching==.

p04-q1.qEn: A client hires your team to design a personalized outfit recommendation algorithm, though they cannot yet clearly define what constitutes a 'great recommendation.' They want to review multiple experimental builds to give feedback and fine-tune model accuracy until they are completely satisfied, then launch once to the live online store. Which approach best describes this strategy?
choicesEn: Predictive (Waterfall)
Iterative
Incremental
Fixed-Scope Sequential
p04-q1.explainEn: Two hallmark indicators of Iterative: (1) cycling through prototypes/builds to refine CORRECTNESS when requirements are ambiguous, and (2) delivering a single formal release at the end once the solution converges.

p04-q2.qEn: A supermarket chain needs to replace its legacy point-of-sale system. Business rules for checkout, inventory, and loyalty cards are already well-defined, but executives need the Checkout module running live after the first 6 weeks, followed by Inventory at week 12, to start realizing ROI early. Which development approach fits best?
choicesEn: Incremental
Predictive with a single delivery after 12 months
Iterative building non-working mockups only
Ad-hoc with no planning
p04-q2.explainEn: Overall requirements are clear, and the top priority is SPEED OF EARLY DELIVERY of complete, immediately usable subsets across successive releases—the defining strength of Incremental.

p04-q3.qEn: An agricultural drone project has two major workstreams: (A) Manufacturing a carbon-fiber airframe and obtaining aviation frequency permits with fixed technical regulations and high tooling costs; (B) Developing a smart flight-path tablet app whose features need testing with farmers every 2 weeks. How should the PM design the approach?
choicesEn: Force both the physical airframe and the software to run pure Scrum, shipping a new airframe every 2 weeks.
Force the entire project into Predictive, locking 100% of the app UI on day one.
Apply a Hybrid model: manage airframe manufacturing & regulatory licensing with Predictive, develop the software with Agile, and establish synchronized Integration Milestones between both streams.
Split into two separate companies that do not communicate.
p04-q3.explainEn: Per PMBOK 8 §4.2, Hybrid is optimal for multi-component projects: physical/regulatory streams with high cost of change use Predictive, software needing rapid feedback uses Agile, and the PM focuses on managing dependencies and syncing integration milestones.

p04-q4.qEn: In an Adaptive / Agile model, how is the relationship among Scope, Schedule, and Finance managed?
choicesEn: Lock 100% of Scope upfront while allowing Schedule and Finance to expand indefinitely.
Fix Time (Timebox) and Cost/team size while keeping Scope flexible and prioritized so the highest-value items are delivered first.
Leave all three constraints floating freely without boundaries.
Eliminate budget and release tracking entirely.
p04-q4.explainEn: Agile inverts the traditional iron triangle: Time (Sprint/Release Timebox) and Cost (stable team) are fixed, while Scope varies by reprioritizing the Product Backlog to maximize delivered value.

p04-q5.qEn: After attending a conference, executives at a traditional insurance corporation (used to strict sign-offs for 20 years) tell the PM to convert a core project to '100% pure paperless Agile starting Monday morning.' Department heads are confused and resistant. What is the BEST recommendation the PM should make?
choicesEn: Execute the directive by deleting all governance documents and reports on Monday morning.
Reject Agile completely and keep 100% of the legacy process.

Assess organizational readiness and propose a phased Hybrid transition roadmap (retaining necessary compliance governance while introducing short iterations alongside Agile training and coaching for the team and stakeholders).
Hire a brand-new development team to replace all current staff.
p04-q5.explainEn: A classic PMP exam scenario! When organizational culture is not ready and compliance demands are high, an abrupt switch causes systemic shock. The PMI standard is Tailoring a transitional Hybrid roadmap paired with training and coaching.

p04-c1.frontEn: What are the 2 core axes of the Stacey Matrix used to select a project development approach?
p04-c1.backEn:
1. Requirements Uncertainty (What are we building?)
2. Technical Uncertainty (How will we build it?)
• Both clear & stable → Predictive.
• Rising uncertainty (Complex zone) → Iterative / Incremental / Agile.

p04-c2.frontEn: What is the 10-second keyword trick to tell 'Iterative' vs. 'Incremental' apart on the PMP exam?
p04-c2.backEn:
• Iterative = Repeat Prototypes/Mockups to optimize CORRECTNESS (clarify fuzzy requirements), single final delivery.
• Incremental = Deliver complete slices to optimize SPEED (users get immediate partial value early).

p04-c3.frontEn: How does the Iron Triangle (Scope · Schedule · Finance) invert when moving from Predictive to Agile?
p04-c3.backEn:
• Predictive: Fix Scope upfront → estimate Schedule & Finance.
• Agile (Adaptive): Fix Schedule (Timebox) & Finance (stable team capacity) → flex and optimize Scope in highest-value order.

p04-c4.frontEn: When is Hybrid the BEST answer on the PMP exam?
p04-c4.backEn:
1. Projects with multiple components of different natures (e.g., stable hardware/construction/regulatory + volatile software/AI).
2. Traditional organizations starting an Agile transformation that need a safe transitional bridge with coaching.

p04-c5.frontEn: How does the 'Planning' Focus Area (of PMBOK 8's 5 Focus Areas) differ between Predictive and Agile?
p04-c5.backEn:
• Predictive: Detailed Upfront Planning at project start and locking Baselines.
• Agile: Continuous multi-horizon adaptive planning (Progressive / Rolling-wave) from Vision → Roadmap → Release → Backlog Refinement → Sprint Planning.

P05.titleEn: Operating Agile & Scrum: Roles, Events & Three Quality Gates (DoR · AC · DoD)
P05.summaryEn: Clarify the strict authority boundaries among Product Owner · Developers · Scrum Master / Agile PM, the inspect-and-adapt essence of the 5 Scrum events, and the 3 core quality gates: Definition of Ready (DoR) · Acceptance Criteria (AC) · Definition of Done (DoD).
P05.mottoEn: PO owns Value · Developers own Volume & How · Scrum Master clears the path & keeps the cadence
P05.realWorldTrapEn: Turning the Daily Standup into a status interrogation for the PM, letting a director message Developers directly to slip new work mid-Sprint, or having the PM reprioritize the Product Backlog instead of the Product Owner.
P05.pmiMindsetShiftEn: Respect ownership boundaries in Scrum absolutely: all external requests must route through the Product Owner; never make changes that endanger the Sprint Goal; Daily Scrum is 15 minutes for Developers to sync their next-24-hour plan; only an Increment meeting the full Definition of Done may be demonstrated and released.

steps.headingEn: Core Concepts in Scrum Operations (Product Backlog, Sprint, Cross-functional Team, Impediment)
steps.bodyEn:
In many real-world companies, Scrum gets practiced inaccurately: a Tech Lead acts as Scrum Master while assigning tasks by KPI, or stakeholders push requests straight into an active Sprint. Applying those flawed habits on the PMP exam leads straight to wrong answers.

Before tackling situational questions, lock in the exact definitions of four core **Scrum** concepts:

- **Product Backlog:** The single ordered queue containing all features, enhancements, and bug fixes for the product, prioritized by **business value and risk**.
- **Sprint (*1–4 week fixed cadence*):** A fixed **Timebox** during which the team converts top-priority items into a working, usable product **Increment**.
- **Cross-functional & T-shaped Team:** A team of 3–9 people possessing all skills (Backend, Frontend, QA, UX...) needed to finish features end-to-end without external handoffs; each member has deep expertise in one specialty (*vertical bar of the T*) and is ready to help with adjacent skills (*horizontal bar of the T*) when needed.
- **Impediment:** Any blocker beyond the team's ability to resolve on its own that interrupts work (e.g., waiting days for the InfoSec team to provision access credentials).

> [!NOTE]

steps.headingEn: Distinguishing the 3 Quality Gates: DoR, Acceptance Criteria, and DoD
steps.bodyEn:
Disagreements over *"whether a work item is actually finished"* usually stem from confusing these three terms. Consider the lifecycle of an **OTP Login** feature:

- **Definition of Ready (`DoR` — Sprint Entry Gate):** Readiness checklist verifying that a User Story on the Product Backlog has clear business rules, UI designs, technical clarity, and small enough size (*INVEST criteria*) before the team pulls it into `Sprint Planning`. *(Teams typically spend up to ~10% of Sprint capacity on **Backlog Refinement** to get stories Ready for upcoming Sprints.)*
- **Acceptance Criteria (`AC` — Story-Specific Pass/Fail Rules):** Functional conditions specific to that single User Story (e.g., *"OTP code expires after exactly 60 seconds; 5 consecutive wrong attempts lock login for 15 minutes"*).
- **Definition of Done (`DoD` — Shared Product-Wide Completion Standard):** Mandatory quality bar applied to **every Increment** before release (Peer Code Review passed, Unit Test coverage threshold met, security scan clean, deployed stably on Staging). ==An item passing AC but failing DoD earns zero Velocity points, cannot be shown at the Sprint Review, and must return to the Product Backlog for the PO to reprioritize.==

```visual
    badge: "Demo phần mềm chạy thật"
    tone: "sky"
    cause: "Mang tính năng dở dang chưa đạt DoD ra báo cáo một chiều, không thu được phản hồi thực tế."
    fix: "Chỉ trình diễn **Working Increment đã đạt 100% DoD**, mời Stakeholders dùng thử trực tiếp và thu thập phản hồi để cập nhật lại Product Backlog."
  - symptom: "Đợi hết dự án 6 tháng mới họp rút kinh nghiệm khiến xung đột và lỗi quy trình tích tụ"
    badge: "Sprint Retrospective"
    tone: "emerald"
    cause: "Thiếu vòng lặp cải tiến quy trình định kỳ trong không gian an toàn tâm lý."
    fix: "Tổ chức **Sprint Retrospective** đều đặn cuối MỖI Sprint để cả nhóm tự nhìn lại cách phối hợp và chọn ngay 1–2 cải tiến khả thi áp dụng vào Sprint kế tiếp."
```

> [!TIP]
> **Quick distinction between Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective:** ==Sprint Review focuses on the PRODUCT== (inspecting the Increment with customers/Stakeholders); ==Sprint Retrospective focuses on PROCESS & PEOPLE== (internal improvement session solely for the Scrum Team).

p05-q1.qEn: A Scrum team is on Day 5 of a 2-week Sprint. The Sales Director walks straight up to a Senior Developer's desk and demands a new analytics chart be added immediately in this Sprint for a partner meeting next week. The Senior Developer is unsettled and escalates to you (Scrum Master / Agile PM). What should you do?
choicesEn: Ask the Senior Developer to work overtime in the evening to add the chart and keep the Sales Director happy.
Delete another User Story from the Sprint Backlog yourself to make room for the new chart.

Protect the team from ad-hoc mid-Sprint interruptions, and speak directly with the Sales Director to guide him to work with the Product Owner to evaluate value and prioritize it on the Product Backlog.
Cancel the current Sprint immediately and replan from scratch.
p05-q1.explainEn: Scrum gold standard: (1) No outsider may inject unvetted work that disrupts Developers mid-Sprint; (2) The Scrum Master acts as a shield protecting the team; (3) All new requests must flow through the single gate—the Product Owner—to be weighed by value on the Product Backlog (only the PO may cancel a Sprint if the goal becomes obsolete).

p05-q2.qEn: You just stepped in as Scrum Master for a team and notice their Daily Standup drags on for 45 minutes every day: two developers routinely argue over SQL query optimization details, while a Legal department representative repeatedly interrupts to ask for weekly progress updates. How should you address this?
choicesEn: Officially extend the Daily Standup to 60 minutes so everyone can finish speaking.

Coach the team on the purpose of Daily Scrum (15 minutes exclusively for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal), move deep technical debates to a separate follow-up session after the meeting, and align with the Legal representative not to interrupt (receiving updates via Sprint Review / Information Radiators instead).
Cancel the Daily Standup altogether and switch to nightly email status reports to the PM.
Forbid the two developers from speaking to each other during the Sprint.
p05-q2.explainEn: Daily Scrum is a 15-minute Timeboxed event BY Developers and FOR Developers to synchronize their next-24-hour plan. Detailed technical problem-solving goes to a 'Parking Lot' (an after-standup huddle for those involved), and external Stakeholders must not turn Daily Scrum into a status interrogation.

p05-q3.qEn: At the end of a Sprint, a User Story passes every business scenario the customer expects for ticket booking (seat selection, promo codes, email delivery). However, the code has not yet passed the automated security scan or received API documentation as required for the whole product. How should the team classify and handle this User Story?
choicesEn: Credit the full Story Points to this Sprint's Velocity and demo it normally because it passed Acceptance Criteria.

Classify it as meeting its individual Acceptance Criteria but NOT the shared Definition of Done (DoD); therefore do NOT count it as complete, do not demo it as finished product, and return the remaining work to the Product Backlog for the PO to prioritize in a future Sprint.
Lower the Definition of Done standard on the last afternoon of the Sprint to report 100% completion.
Assign the Product Owner to write the API documentation and run the security scan.
p05-q3.explainEn: Classic test distinguishing Acceptance Criteria (story-specific business conditions) from Definition of Done (shared quality bar for every Increment). Without 100% DoD compliance, no compliant Increment exists: never inflate Velocity or demo unfinished work!

p05-q4.qEn: During Sprint Planning, the Developers repeatedly waste 3–4 hours confused because the top User Stories in the Product Backlog are oversized, vague, and have unclear technical dependencies. What root-cause fix prevents this in future Sprints?
choicesEn: Have the Scrum Master write all User Stories and pre-estimate them before the meeting.
Establish a recurring Backlog Refinement cadence with the Product Owner and apply Definition of Ready (DoR / INVEST) criteria to clarify and split high-priority items before Sprint Planning.
Skip Sprint Planning altogether and just pick whatever easy tasks are available.
Extend Sprint Planning to 3 consecutive days.
p05-q4.explainEn: The symptom 'Sprint Planning stalls because stories are too big and ambiguous' is a textbook sign of missing Backlog Refinement and a missing Definition of Ready (DoR) entry gate.

p05-q5.qEn: Midway through Sprint 4, due to a corporate strategy pivot, the company unexpectedly announces the complete discontinuation of the product line that the current Sprint Goal is building. Who holds the official authority to cancel this active Sprint?
choicesEn: Scrum Master
QA Lead
Product Owner
Any Developer on the team
p05-q5.explainEn: Per the Scrum Guide and PMP standards, ONLY the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete (though the PO may take input from Stakeholders, Developers, or the Scrum Master).

p05-q6.qEn: In an Agile project, the Sprint Review is the event where the team reflects on internal collaboration, team morale, and improving its testing workflow for the next Sprint.
p05-q6.explainEn: False! The Sprint Review focuses on the PRODUCT (inspecting the Working Increment with Stakeholders and adapting the Product Backlog). Reflecting on PEOPLE, RELATIONSHIPS, and internal WORK PROCESSES is the Sprint Retrospective.

p05-c1.frontEn: Summarize the authority boundaries of the 3 Scrum roles (PO · Developers · Scrum Master) in 3 lines.
p05-c1.backEn:
• Product Owner (PO): Owns the Product Backlog, maximizes VALUE (Why/What), sole authority to cancel a Sprint.
• Developers: Estimate effort (How much), decide technical approach (How), own the Sprint Backlog.
• Scrum Master: Servant Leader who coaches the process, removes Impediments, and shields the team from external noise.

p05-c2.frontEn: Clearly distinguish the purpose of 'Sprint Review' vs. 'Sprint Retrospective'.
p05-c2.backEn:
• Sprint Review = Inspect the PRODUCT (demo DoD-compliant Increment to Stakeholders for feedback to update Product Backlog).
• Sprint Retrospective = Inspect internal TEAM PROCESS & PEOPLE (pick 1–2 actionable improvements for the very next Sprint).

p05-c3.frontEn: Distinguish the 3 quality gates: DoR · Acceptance Criteria (AC) · DoD.
p05-c3.backEn:
• DoR (Definition of Ready): ENTRY gate ensuring a Story is clear/small enough before Sprint Planning.
• AC (Acceptance Criteria): SPECIFIC business pass/fail rules for an individual User Story.
• DoD (Definition of Done): SHARED quality standard required of EVERY Increment to be deemed complete & releasable.

p05-c4.frontEn: When a Stakeholder demands squeezing an urgent feature into an active Sprint, what is the PMI-aligned response?
p05-c4.backEn: The Scrum Master / Agile PM protects the team's focus, explains the rule against disrupting the Sprint Goal, and guides the Stakeholder to work directly with the Product Owner to assess value and prioritize it into the Product Backlog for an upcoming Sprint.

p05-c5.frontEn: What happens to a User Story that is 90% done (not fully meeting Definition of Done) when the Sprint ends?
p05-c5.backEn:
• Do NOT demo it as completed work at the Sprint Review.
• Award ZERO Story Points toward that Sprint's Velocity.
• Return it to the Product Backlog for the Product Owner to re-prioritize and re-estimate the remaining work for a future Sprint.

p05-c6.frontEn: What is the golden rule of the Daily Scrum (Daily Standup) on the PMP exam?
p05-c6.backEn: Strictly Timeboxed to 15 minutes, for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and plan the next 24 hours of coordination. NEVER turn it into a status report to the PM or deep-dive technical debugging (move those to a post-standup Parking Lot).

P06.titleEn: Adaptive Planning, Kanban WIP Limits & Hybrid Project Coordination
P06.summaryEn: Master rolling planning cadences (Progressive Elaboration & Rolling Wave), protect the transparency of Story Points & Velocity, unblock Kanban pull flow using WIP limits, and smoothly coordinate Hybrid projects or organizational Agile transformations.
P06.mottoEn: Forecast with Velocity · Limit WIP to Flow · Tailor Hybrid by Context
P06.realWorldTrapEn: Using Team A's Velocity as a KPI to compare against Team B, pressuring developers to inflate Velocity every Sprint, or forcing an immediate full-scale shift to Agile regardless of hardware and regulatory constraints.
P06.pmiMindsetShiftEn: Velocity is strictly an internal capacity-forecasting metric for a SINGLE team; to finish work faster in Kanban, REDUCE the WIP limit (Stop starting, start finishing); transitioning to Agile must proceed incrementally via a Hybrid model accompanied by training and coaching.

steps.headingEn: Kanban Pull Mechanism and Work-in-Progress (WIP) Limits
steps.bodyEn:
Consider a common scenario on a software development team: a backend developer takes on **5 parallel work items** at once (`WIP = 5` — *Work in Progress*, meaning tasks started but not yet finished). While simultaneously writing a payment API, helping troubleshoot order bugs, attending cart clarification meetings, and handling urgent hotfixes, the developer loses most of their time to **context switching**. As a result, the `QA Testing` column piles up with cards waiting to be tested, and the time required to complete a single feature stretches across many days.

**Kanban** solves this multitasking overload through a **Pull System** built on the core principle of ==WIP Limits (capping the maximum number of work items allowed in progress simultaneously in each column)==. The mathematical foundation behind this principle is **Little's Law**:

- **Formula:** `Cycle Time (Time to complete 1 item) = WIP (Items currently in progress) / Throughput (Average delivery rate)`.
- **Operational implication:** When a team's average capacity remains constant, ==the most effective way to shorten the time needed to finish each feature (Cycle Time) is to reduce the amount of work in progress (WIP)== rather than increasing overtime hours.
- **How to respond when hitting a WIP cap:** If the `Testing` column has `WIP Limit = 3` and already holds `3/3` cards, a developer who finishes coding a 4th card **must not push it into Testing** and **must not pull a new card to start**; instead, the whole team collaborates to clear the testing bottleneck (*Swarming — "Stop starting, start finishing"*).

steps.headingEn: Rolling Wave Planning, Story Points, and Principles for Using Velocity
steps.bodyEn:
In high-uncertainty environments, the project team plans using two [!badge:amber:PMBOK 8] techniques: **Progressive Elaboration** (*iteratively refining details as real data emerges*) and **Rolling Wave Planning** (*planning the next 1–2 near-term iterations in detail while keeping later phases at a high level*).

When estimating Agile work, instead of estimating absolute hours—which are prone to bias—the development team uses relative sizing with **Story Points** (reflecting a composite of 3 factors: **Logical complexity · Amount of work · Risk/uncertainty**) via **Planning Poker** or **Affinity Estimating**. The total Story Points of backlog items that **fully satisfy 100% of the DoD** within a Sprint is called **Velocity** (*the team's average completion rate*).

```visual
    - "PM tự ước lượng điểm hoặc yêu cầu nhóm tăng Velocity thêm 20% ở Sprint tiếp theo."
```

> [!WARNING]
> **Exam alert on requests to increase Velocity:** When a question asks how to improve an Agile team's rate of value delivery, eliminate options such as *"require overtime"* or *"mandate higher Velocity targets"*. The correct approach is to ==remove systemic impediments, automate testing/CI/CD to reduce technical debt, and minimize multitasking==.

Consider a Self-Service Banking Kiosk project (**Hybrid**): the hardware manufacturing team (enclosure and card reader) operates on a fixed 6-month **Predictive** schedule, while the facial-recognition software team works in **2-week Agile Sprints**.
