> **Decision rules for Kanban & Hybrid:** When a queue backs up at a workflow stage → ==tighten the WIP Limit and rally the team to swarm and clear the bottleneck in place==; when Predictive and Agile tracks risk drifting out of phase → ==establish Shared Integration Milestones and hold cross-team synchronization meetings==.

p06-q1.qEn: The PMO Director notices that Team Alpha averages 65 Story Points per Sprint, whereas Team Beta working on a similar project achieves only 32 Story Points. The Director asks you—the Agile Project Manager—to instruct Team Beta to raise their Velocity to match Team Alpha. How should you respond?
choicesEn: Hold a meeting requiring Team Beta to commit to increasing their Velocity by at least 10 Story Points each Sprint until they match Team Alpha.
Explain to the Director that Story Points and Velocity are relative internal metrics specific to each team and cannot be used to compare performance across two different teams.
Require the Scrum Masters of both teams to convert all Story Points into standardized man-hours for a fair comparison.
Transfer two top developers from Team Alpha to Team Beta to balance out the Velocity scores.
p06-q1.explainEn: Under PMI Agile standards, each team defines its own Story Point reference scale. Velocity is used solely to forecast a single team's internal capacity across Sprints; it must never be used as a cross-team comparison KPI or rigidly converted into individual man-hours.

p06-q2.qEn: A development team operates using a Kanban board. Recently, average feature Cycle Time has doubled. On the Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD), the color band for the 'Integration Testing' column is widening continuously and has hit its maximum WIP limit, yet developers keep pulling new cards into the 'In Development' column. What should you guide the team to do NEXT?
choicesEn: Double the WIP limit on the Integration Testing column so developers are not blocked from pushing work forward.
Stop pulling new cards into In Development and mobilize the entire team to swarm and resolve the bottleneck in Integration Testing.
Ask HR to hire temporary QA contractors immediately this week.
Skip several non-critical regression tests to drain the queue faster.
p06-q2.explainEn: In a Kanban pull system, WIP limits exist to expose bottlenecks. Raising the WIP limit only bloats the queue further and worsens Cycle Time; cutting quality violates Principle #3. The right reflex is 'Stop starting, start finishing'—having the whole team swarm to clear the bottleneck before pulling new work.

p06-q3.qEn: You are managing a smart medical device project: the mechanical enclosure and safety certification must follow a fixed design with sequential approval gates, whereas the mobile data-analytics app requires biweekly testing and iteration with physicians. Which management approach is MOST appropriate?
choicesEn: Pure Predictive for the entire project because healthcare is heavily regulated.
Pure 2-week Scrum for both the mechanical and software teams to standardize ways of working.
A Hybrid model: manage hardware and regulatory compliance using Predictive milestones, while developing the mobile app in Agile iterations synchronized at shared integration milestones.
Split them into two completely independent projects with zero communication until product launch day.
p06-q3.explainEn: This is a classic PMBOK 8 Tailoring & Hybrid scenario: select the fitting methodology per component based on requirement uncertainty and compliance constraints, while the PM acts as the bridge synchronizing cross-team integration milestones.

p06-q4.qEn: At the end of Sprint 4, a User Story estimated at 8 Story Points has 95% of its code completed, but one criterion in the Definition of Done (automated security testing) has not finished running. How should the team handle this item's points in Sprint 4 Velocity?
choicesEn: Credit 7 Story Points to Sprint 4 Velocity and carry the remaining 1 point over to Sprint 5.
Count 0 points for this User Story toward Sprint 4 Velocity and return the item to the Product Backlog for the Product Owner to prioritize for the next Sprint.
Extend Sprint 4 by 1 day to finish running the security tests and claim all 8 points.
Ask the Product Owner for conditional sign-off to keep the Velocity chart looking good.
p06-q4.explainEn: Agile applies a binary completion rule: if an item does not satisfy 100% of the Definition of Done, it does not form a safely usable Increment, so 0 Story Points are counted toward the current Sprint's Velocity, and the Sprint Timebox is never extended.

p06-q5.qEn: A financial corporation accustomed to Waterfall for 15 years wants to transition to Agile. On the first pilot project, both the project team and functional managers feel confused and resistant because they sense a loss of control without an annual detailed Gantt chart. As the Project Manager leading this initiative, what is the BEST strategy?
choicesEn: Issue a strict mandate abolishing all legacy planning documents immediately and penalize anyone who does not follow Scrum.
Revert 100% back to Waterfall because financial corporate culture can never fit Agile.
Adopt a gradual transition roadmap via a Hybrid model paired with Agile mindset training and coaching for both the team and stakeholders.
Escalate to the Executive Board requesting the replacement of conservative functional managers.
p06-q5.explainEn: Organizational Agile transformation is an Organizational Change Management (OCM) journey. PMI consistently favors a Hybrid stepping-stone paired with coaching/training to build psychological safety and incremental adaptation rather than abrupt coercion or giving up.

p06-q6.qEn: In Rolling Wave Planning, work packages scheduled for the near term are planned in detail, while work further out in the future is kept at a high level (Planning Packages) until clearer information becomes available.
p06-q6.explainEn: Correct! Rolling Wave Planning is a specific form of Progressive Elaboration that prevents wasting effort guessing fine-grained details too early for work many months away.

p06-c1.frontEn: Why must you NEVER use Velocity to compare productivity between two Agile teams?
p06-c1.backEn: Because Story Points are relative estimates calibrated to each team's own baseline. Comparing Velocity across teams distorts data, causes point inflation, and destroys forecasting transparency.

p06-c2.frontEn: What is the core purpose of setting a WIP (Work in Progress) Limit on a Kanban board?
p06-c2.backEn: To reduce context-switching waste, shorten Cycle Time per Little's Law, and expose bottlenecks clearly so the entire team can swarm to clear the queue.

p06-c3.frontEn: What key advantage does a Burnup chart have over a Burndown chart when reporting Release progress?
p06-c3.backEn: A Burnup chart separates the 'Total Scope' line from the 'Completed Work' line, making it immediately obvious whether a missed target is due to slower team pace or newly added scope.

p06-c4.frontEn: On a Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD), what visual sign indicates a bottleneck at a workflow stage?
p06-c4.backEn: The color band for that state widens vertically (WIP piling up) while its lower boundary flattens or goes horizontal (slow outflow).

p06-c5.frontEn: When a long-standing Predictive organization wants to adopt Agile but faces resistance, which path should the PM choose?
p06-c5.backEn: Apply a phased transition via a Hybrid model (keeping familiar Governance checkpoints for leadership while introducing Agile/Kanban practices to the team) supported by training and coaching.

p06-c6.frontEn: If a User Story is 90% done when the Sprint Timebox expires, how many points count toward Velocity?
p06-c6.backEn: 0 points! Agile only credits Velocity for items that meet 100% of the Definition of Done; unfinished work returns to the Product Backlog for the PO to reprioritize.

P07.titleEn: Governance Domain: Project Charter, Change Control (CCB) & Data Flow
P07.summaryEn: Master PMBOK 8 Performance Domain #1 Governance (9 processes): formal authorization via the Project Charter, the invariant Change Request sequence through the CCB, transforming raw data into reports (WPD → WPI → WPR), knowledge management, and proper project closure.
P07.mottoEn: Charter Grants Authority · Assess Before CCB · Follow WPD → WPI → WPR
P07.realWorldTrapEn: Letting the team start execution before the Project Charter is signed; updating the Baseline directly or rushing to the CCB before performing impact analysis when a client requests a change; disbanding the team immediately without formal closure when a project is cancelled mid-way.
P07.pmiMindsetShiftEn: The Sponsor-signed Project Charter is the sole formal document granting authority to the PM; once Baselines are locked, every change must follow 'Log → Assess Impact → Submit to CCB → Update Plan & Communicate'; even an early-terminated project must go through Close Project to archive Lessons Learned and close contracts.

steps.headingEn: Role of the Project Charter and Change Approval Authority (CCB vs Product Owner)
steps.bodyEn:
In **PMBOK® Guide 8 (`§2.1`)**, the **Governance** domain (*9 processes*) serves as the legal framework and control mechanism for the entire project. Two areas that commonly cause confusion are the true role of the **Project Charter** and the boundary between changes requiring the **Change Control Board (CCB)** versus those approved by the **Product Owner**.

- **Project Charter:** The formal document **issued and signed by the Project Sponsor** that authorizes the project's existence and grants the PM legitimate authority to apply organizational budget, infrastructure, and cross-functional staff (often likened to the project's birth certificate). With only a verbal assignment and no `Project Charter`, the PM lacks formal authority to mobilize resources from other departments.
- **Change Approval Authority — `CCB` (*Change Control Board*) vs `Product Owner` (`PO`):**
  - **Submit to the `CCB` via `PICC` (*Perform Integrated Change Control*):** Applies when the project uses **Predictive** delivery (or the fixed-contract portion of a **Hybrid** project) and the **`Scope / Schedule / Cost Baseline` is locked**. Any change shifting a committed baseline must undergo formal CCB review.
  - **Handled solely by `Product Owner` adjusting the `Product Backlog` (NO CCB needed):** Applies when feature changes sit within an **Agile** project (where Timebox and Budget stay fixed while detailed scope flexes by value). However, in a Hybrid project, if a change impacts **contractual milestones or exceeds the overall budget ceiling**, CCB/Sponsor approval is still mandatory.


steps.headingEn: Close Project or Phase Process
steps.bodyEn:
A common misconception is that once the customer signs off on acceptance—or when a project is cancelled mid-stream—team members can be released immediately without executing formal closure.

> [!TIP]
> **Mandatory rules for Project Closure (including early termination):**
> 1. Confirm formal acceptance of deliverables (`Accepted Deliverables`) or inventory all work completed up to the stop point and document the exact termination rationale.
> 2. Transition deliverables to **Operations**, complete contract closeout, and assess stakeholder satisfaction.
> 3. Archive insights from the *Lessons Learned Register* into **Organizational Process Assets (*OPA*)**, issue the *Final Report*, and ==release project team resources as the final step==.

p07-q1.qEn: The executive board has just approved the Business Case for an ERP upgrade project. A finance manager urges you—who have just been tapped as Project Manager—to assign three engineers immediately this week to audit server configurations. Currently, the Project Charter is still sitting on the Sponsor's desk awaiting signature. What should you do FIRST?
choicesEn: Assign the three engineers right away to build goodwill with the finance manager while waiting for the signature.
Begin drafting the Project Management Plan and breaking down a detailed WBS immediately.
Explain that the project has not yet received formal authorization and work with the Sponsor to finalize and sign the Project Charter before mobilizing execution resources.
Ask the finance manager to submit a Change Request to the CCB to borrow the engineers.
p07-q1.explainEn: A Sponsor-signed Project Charter is the sole document that formally authorizes a project and grants the PM authority to use organizational resources. Without a signed Charter, the PM cannot unilaterally deploy execution resources.

p07-q2.qEn: A data center construction project is in month 5 (all 3 Baselines are locked). A key client emails requesting an upgrade to a higher-tier cooling system to prepare for AI servers. As the Project Manager, what is your NEXT action?
choicesEn: Forward the email directly to the Change Control Board (CCB) so they can vote on it.
Update the Scope Baseline and Cost Baseline right away to reflect the client's reasonable request.
Work with the project team to conduct a comprehensive impact analysis across scope, schedule, cost, risk, and quality before submitting a Change Request to the CCB.
Reject the request outright because Predictive projects prohibit changes after baselines are locked.
p07-q2.explainEn: The standard PMI sequence is always: Assess impact with the team first → Log a formal Change Request → Submit to the CCB with analysis data. Going to the CCB without impact data or altering baselines unilaterally both violate process.

p07-q3.qEn: In your monthly report to the Steering Committee, you attach a Dashboard summarizing overall project health (RAG status), Earned Value trend charts, and recommended corrective actions. In PMI data-flow terminology, what is this document called?
choicesEn: Work Performance Data (WPD)
Work Performance Information (WPI)
Work Performance Reports (WPR)
Project Charter Updates
p07-q3.explainEn: WPD consists of raw measurements gathered during execution; WPI is the analyzed variance against Baselines within individual control processes; WPR (Work Performance Reports) is the consolidated document/dashboard packaging WPI to communicate and support decisions by stakeholders/CCB.

p07-q4.qEn: A lead architect with 20 years of tenure is about to retire and holds vast undocumented troubleshooting experience. Which method is MOST EFFECTIVE for capturing and transferring this valuable Tacit Knowledge to the project and organization?
choicesEn: Ask the architect to sit down and type a 300-page manual during their final week.
Organize pairing sessions (shadowing/mentoring), real-world case workshops, and direct knowledge-sharing conversations with successor engineers paired with key-takeaway notes.
Email a multiple-choice survey for the architect to complete before returning their laptop.
Archive all of the architect's legacy source code onto a shared drive without further discussion.
p07-q4.explainEn: Tacit Knowledge (intuition, nuanced context, hands-on problem-solving judgment) is difficult to capture purely in dry text; the best transfer mechanism is direct social interaction such as shadowing, mentoring, storytelling, and collaborative practice.

p07-q5.qEn: Due to exchange-rate volatility and a merger strategy shift, the Sponsor sends written notice terminating your project halfway through execution. What should you do with the team and project records?
choicesEn: Release all staff back to their functional departments this afternoon to maximize budget savings.

Execute the Close Project or Phase process: verify and hand over completed deliverables to date, document the termination rationale, archive Lessons Learned in OPA, close contracts, and only then release the team.
Keep running the project using contingency reserves until at least one more phase finishes.
Delete incomplete documentation since the project never reached its final goal.
p07-q5.explainEn: When a project is terminated early, the PM is STILL REQUIRED to perform formal closure to investigate/document the reasons for termination, formally transfer valid partial deliverables, close vendor contracts, and archive lessons learned into OPA before releasing staff.

p07-q6.qEn: When the Change Control Board (CCB) decides to REJECT a Change Request, the Project Manager does not need to record that request in the Change Log so as to avoid cluttering project records.
p07-q6.explainEn: False! Every Change Request—whether pending, approved, deferred, or REJECTED—must have its status and rationale updated in the Change Log to maintain transparency and prevent duplicate proposals from resurfacing.

p07-c1.frontEn: Which document formally initiates a project and grants the Project Manager authority to apply organizational resources? Who signs it?
p07-c1.backEn: The Project Charter — must be signed and issued by the Project Sponsor or an external authorizing entity.

p07-c2.frontEn: What is the invariant 5-step sequence for handling a change request that touches a locked Baseline?
p07-c2.backEn: 1. Analyze impact with the team → 2. Create Change Request & log in Change Log → 3. Submit to CCB for decision → 4. Update Baselines/PM Plan & Change Log → 5. Communicate & implement.

p07-c3.frontEn: Distinguish WPD · WPI · WPR in 10 seconds!
p07-c3.backEn: WPD = Raw field measurements (uncompared); WPI = Analyzed variance against Baseline (e.g., CPI=0.88); WPR = Consolidated reports/dashboards built from WPI for stakeholder decision-making.

p07-c4.frontEn: In PMBOK® Guide 8, which areas from prior editions are consolidated into Performance Domain #1 Governance?
p07-c4.backEn: It combines all of legacy Project Integration Management plus Manage Quality Assurance (QA) and Plan Sourcing Strategy (high-level procurement strategy) into 9 processes.

p07-c5.frontEn: What is the core difference between Explicit Knowledge and Tacit Knowledge in Manage Project Knowledge?
p07-c5.backEn: Explicit knowledge is easily codified into text, numbers, and procedures; Tacit knowledge consists of deep craft experience and subtle context, best transferred via dialogue, mentoring, and working side-by-side.

p07-c6.frontEn: What is the final action in the Close Project or Phase sequence (and does it apply to early-cancelled projects)?
p07-c6.backEn: Applies to BOTH completed and early-cancelled projects! Hand over current deliverables/assets, close contracts, update Lessons Learned in OPA, issue the Final Report, and ONLY THEN release team members.

P08.titleEn: Stakeholders & Communications: Stakeholder Analysis, SEAM & Channels
P08.summaryEn: Master PMBOK 8 Performance Domain #5 Stakeholders (7 processes uniting Stakeholder Engagement & Communications): Power/Interest and Salience Model classification, shifting attitudes on the SEAM matrix, selecting among the 3 communication methods, and avoiding the Stakeholder Plan vs Communications Plan trap.
P08.mottoEn: Identify Early · Shift Attitude via SEAM · Right Message via Right Channel
P08.realWorldTrapEn: Avoiding a resistant department head by excluding them from meetings or asking the Sponsor to overrule them; relying on long emails to resolve sensitive issues; confusing updates to the Stakeholder Engagement Plan with the Communications Management Plan.
P08.pmiMindsetShiftEn: The higher a Resistant stakeholder's power, the more proactively the PM must meet 1-on-1 to uncover root concerns and shift them toward Supportive; issues of ATTITUDE/RELATIONSHIP → update the Stakeholder Engagement Plan; issues of REPORT FORMAT/FREQUENCY/CHANNEL → update the Communications Management Plan.

steps.headingEn: Identifying Stakeholders, the Power/Interest Grid, and the SEAM Matrix
steps.bodyEn:
When rolling out a new Warehouse Management System to replace legacy workflows, many PMs focus solely on reporting to budget-approving executives while neglecting frontline operators (such as warehouse clerks or inventory accountants). Once live operations approach, those end users may push back out of fear that the new workflow adds complexity or exposes past discrepancies, stalling the project.

In **PMBOK® Guide 8 (`§2.5`)**, PMI merges **Stakeholder Engagement** and **Communications** into a single domain called **Stakeholders** (7 processes). Master these 3 core concepts:

- **Stakeholder:** Any individual or organization that impacts the project, is affected by the project, or **perceives themselves to be affected** (from the Sponsor, Dev team, and Legal to end users). Identification (`Identify Stakeholders`) must start **at project initiation and repeat continuously** at phase transitions.
- **Power / Interest Grid:** Classifies stakeholders into 4 quadrants to allocate effort wisely: *High Power + High Interest → `Manage Closely`*; *High Power + Low Interest → `Keep Satisfied` (avoid drowning them in details)*; *Low Power + High Interest → `Keep Informed`*; *Low Power + Low Interest → `Monitor`*.
- **SEAM (*Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix*):** A 5-column attitude tracking table marking **`C` (*Current* attitude)** and **`D` (*Desired* attitude)** so the PM can ==proactively design actions to move C toward D==!

Follow the exact 4 steps: ==(1) Record them in the Stakeholder Register → (2) Analyze power, interest, and current attitude → (3) Update the Stakeholder Engagement Plan & Communications Plan → (4) Proactively meet and engage==.

steps.headingEn: Communication Channels Formula and the 3 PMI Communication Methods
steps.bodyEn:
As project team size and stakeholder count grow, communication complexity increases quadratically according to **Number of channels = `N × (N - 1) / 2`** (where `N` is the total number of participants, making sure to include the PM if not already counted). For example, a 5-person group has `5 × 4 / 2 = 10 channels`, whereas growing to `N = 10` jumps to **`10 × 9 / 2 = 45 channels`**.

steps.headingEn: Real-World Scenario and Decision Rule Between the Two Plans
steps.bodyEn:
Suppose you send PDF progress reports reliably every Monday morning, yet the Operations Director repeatedly rejects the product in month-end reviews, claiming the team does not understand his warehouse processes.

> [!TIP]
> **Quick differentiation rule:**
> - If the issue is that ==reports are delivered reliably yet the recipient resists, stays indifferent, or has misaligned expectations== → Meet face-to-face to listen and update the **Stakeholder Engagement Plan**.
> - If the issue is that ==they are supportive in spirit but miss progress updates because reports are hard to parse, sent via the wrong channel, or omit recipients== → Update the **Communications Management Plan**.

p08-q1.qEn: Midway through execution, the company appoints a new Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) with veto authority over all production releases. This CISO was not previously listed among project stakeholders. As Project Manager, what should you do FIRST?
choicesEn: Email all 50 meeting minutes from project start to present so the CISO can read through them.
Add the new CISO to the Stakeholder Register and analyze their power, interest, and expectations before updating the engagement plan and scheduling an introductory meeting.
Ask the Project Sponsor to speak privately with the CISO and request that they not interfere with the schedule.
Submit a Change Request to the CCB to push the release date back by 1 month in case of a security audit.
p08-q1.explainEn: Whenever a new stakeholder emerges at any point, the standard workflow always begins with Identify Stakeholders: log them in the Stakeholder Register and analyze their attributes/power/interest to form the basis for updating engagement and communication plans.

p08-q2.qEn: A Warehouse Manager (who holds high authority over adoption of the new system) receives every weekly progress report in full, yet repeatedly refuses to assign staff for testing and makes negative remarks claiming the new software will disrupt warehouse operations. Which document should you review and update to address the root cause?
choicesEn: Communications Management Plan — increase email report frequency from weekly to daily.
Stakeholder Engagement Plan — meet directly to understand the root cause of resistance and design a strategy to shift their attitude from Resistant to Supportive.
Scope Baseline — remove the Warehouse module from project scope to avoid friction.
Resource Management Plan — hire external contractors to replace warehouse staff.
p08-q2.explainEn: The manager already receives full information (not a reporting-channel failure); the root issue is a Resistant ATTITUDE on the SEAM matrix. Sending more emails will not help; the PM must meet directly to uncover concerns and update the strategy in the Stakeholder Engagement Plan.

p08-q3.qEn: During a quarterly review, the VP of Finance complains that the project team's 25-page technical weekly reports make it impossible for her to quickly locate the disbursement metrics and cash-flow forecasts she needs for decision-making. What is the Project Manager's BEST action?
choicesEn: Review and update the Communications Management Plan to tailor the content and summary format (Executive Summary) to match the finance executive's information needs.
Update the Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix because the VP of Finance is opposing the project.
Stop sending reports to the VP of Finance to avoid bothering her.
Ask the chief accountant to read the 25-page report every week and summarize it verbally for her.
p08-q3.explainEn: The issue lies in the FORMAT and LEVEL OF DETAIL of the information failing to match the recipient's information needs, which sits squarely inside the Communications Management Plan.

p08-q4.qEn: A project team initially has 6 people and adds 4 integration specialists, bringing the total number of direct communicators on the team to 10. By how many channels has the potential number of communication channels $N(N-1)/2$ increased?
choicesEn: Increased by 4 channels (from 6 to 10).
Increased by 30 channels (from 15 channels to 45 channels).
Increased by 45 channels (from 15 channels to 60 channels).
Increased by 15 channels (from 30 channels to 45 channels).
p08-q4.explainEn: With 6 people: 6 × 5 / 2 = 15 channels. With 10 people: 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 channels. Therefore, the added communication channels = 45 − 15 = 30 channels (tripling the original count, demanding a much tighter communications plan!).

p08-q5.qEn: Your digital transformation project is about to release a 400-page self-service process handbook along with a library of demo videos for 3,500 branch employees nationwide to consult whenever they encounter a relevant task. Which communication method is most appropriate?
choicesEn: Interactive Communication — schedule mandatory 1-on-1 online calls for every employee.
Push Communication — attach a 2GB archive and email it individually to all 3,500 employees.
Pull Communication — publish the materials on an internal Knowledge Portal / Intranet with search functionality and share the access link.
Word-of-mouth updates via team leads during lunch breaks.
p08-q5.explainEn: When information volume is large and a massive audience (3,500 people) needs on-demand self-service lookup as needs arise, Pull Communication (knowledge portal/Intranet/e-learning) is the exact right choice.

p08-q6.qEn: On the Power/Interest Grid, for stakeholders with High Power but Low Interest in day-to-day details, the standard strategy is 'Keep Satisfied'—keeping them satisfied at key milestones without overwhelming them with minor daily updates.
p08-q6.explainEn: Correct! High Power / Low Interest stakeholders (such as senior legal or finance executives) can block the project if dissatisfied, so they should be Kept Satisfied with concise, high-level milestone updates.

p08-c1.frontEn: What are the 5 attitude levels in order on the SEAM (Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix)?

p08-c2.frontEn: What are the 4 strategic quadrants on the Power/Interest Grid for each Power × Interest combination?
p08-c2.backEn:
• High Power + High Interest → Manage Closely
• High Power + Low Interest → Keep Satisfied
• Low Power + High Interest → Keep Informed
• Low Power + Low Interest → Monitor

p08-c3.frontEn: What is the 1-sentence rule to distinguish when to update the Stakeholder Engagement Plan vs the Communications Management Plan?
p08-c3.backEn: Issues with ATTITUDE / RESISTANCE / TRUST → fix the Stakeholder Engagement Plan; Issues with CHANNEL / FREQUENCY / FORMAT / MISSED REPORTS → fix the Communications Management Plan.

p08-c4.frontEn: Distinguish the 3 communication methods: Interactive · Push · Pull!
p08-c4.backEn:
• Interactive: Real-time two-way exchange (meetings, calls — for complex/sensitive topics).
• Push: One-way delivery to specific recipients (emails, reports, memos).
• Pull: Central repository where large audiences retrieve info on demand (Wiki, Intranet, Portal).

p08-c5.frontEn: What is the formula for total potential communication channels given N stakeholders (including the PM)?
p08-c5.backEn: N × (N − 1) / 2. For example: 8 people → 8 × 7 / 2 = 28 communication channels.

p08-c6.frontEn: Which 3 attributes does the Salience Model use to classify stakeholders?
p08-c6.backEn: Power (ability to impose their will) · Urgency (need for immediate attention) · Legitimacy (appropriateness of their involvement).

P09.titleEn: Resources & Team Domain: Tuckman Model, Emotional Intelligence (EI) & Conflict Resolution
P09.summaryEn: Master PMBOK 8 Performance Domain #6 Resources (5 processes centered on 'Lead the Team'): co-create the Team Charter from the start, adapt leadership styles across Tuckman's 5 stages, apply Emotional Intelligence (EI) & intrinsic motivation, engage Virtual Teams, and resolve conflicts the PMI way.
P09.mottoEn: Co-create Team Charter · Adapt Style by Tuckman · Collaborate to Win-Win
P09.realWorldTrapEn: The PM unilaterally drafts and imposes rules on the team; sees two engineers arguing and immediately sends a warning email to the whole group or escalates to HR/Functional Manager; sees a slow-performing member and demands a replacement instead of coaching them.
P09.pmiMindsetShiftEn: The Team Charter (Ground Rules) must be co-created and agreed upon by the ENTIRE TEAM; when healthy conflict arises, let team members try to resolve it first → if it escalates, meet privately 1-on-1 to listen, then guide toward Collaborate / Problem Solve (Win-Win) based on objective data.

steps.headingEn: Team Charter and How It Differs from the Project Charter
steps.bodyEn:
When assembling a technical team with members from different departments or work habits, early friction in collaboration is common: differing work hours, slow code review turnaround times, or inconsistent ways of giving technical feedback.

In **PMBOK® Guide 8 (`§2.6` — Resources Domain, `Lead the Team` process)**, the foundational tool for establishing self-discipline from day one is the **Team Charter** (*also known as a Social Contract / Ground Rules*):

- **Distinction from the `Project Charter`:** While the `Project Charter` is signed by the Sponsor to authorize the project and grant authority to the PM, ==the Team Charter is co-created and agreed upon by all team members==.
- **Core contents:** Defines shared working hours (*Core Hours*), standards for respectful communication during technical debates, code review turnaround commitments, and voting/decision mechanisms when disagreements arise. When the team itself participates in setting the rules, voluntary compliance is far higher than with top-down mandates.

steps.headingEn: Tuckman's 5-Stage Team Development Model and Matching Leadership Styles
steps.bodyEn:
Psychologist Bruce Tuckman demonstrated that every team progresses through **5 stages of development**. The PM must ==flexibly adapt their leadership style to match each stage of team maturity==:

- **Forming → Directing:** When members first start working together, they tend to be cautious and reliant on the PM's coordination. Here, the PM clarifies project goals and facilitates the team in co-creating the `Team Charter`.
- **Storming → Coaching:** As actual work gets underway, disagreements emerge over technical solutions or collaboration methods. This is a normal phase of team growth; the PM listens, maintains psychological safety, and coaches the team to resolve disagreements using objective data.
- **Norming → Supporting:** Team members begin to understand each other's rhythm and proactively follow agreed conventions like code reviews. The PM steps back slightly to encourage trust and autonomy.
- **Performing → Delegating:** The team operates smoothly like a self-organizing unit. The PM delegates technical decisions to the fullest extent and focuses on removing external strategic impediments.
- **Adjourning → Recognizing & Transitioning:** As the project closes, the PM celebrates achievements and helps members transition smoothly to their next assignments.

> [!WARNING]
> **Classic exam trap on team dynamics:** Suppose your team is running smoothly at the `Performing` stage, and suddenly the customer expands the scope so the company adds **2 brand-new developers** to the team (or removes 1 key member). Which stage does the team move to? The required answer is ==back to the Forming stage== — because interpersonal dynamics and working agreements must be re-established from scratch!

steps.headingEn: Five Conflict Resolution Techniques and Supporting Underperforming Team Members
steps.bodyEn:
When two senior engineers strongly disagree over choosing a database or system architecture, the PM needs to master the **3-step escalation ladder** and the **5 conflict resolution techniques**:

```visual
kind: anatomy
title: "Thang Can thiệp 3 Bước & 5 Chế độ Xử lý Xung đột Chuẩn PMI"
subtitle: "Khoảng 90% câu hỏi xung đột trong đề PMP có đáp án đúng là Collaborate / Problem Solve!"
items:
  - keyword: "Thang can thiệp 3 Bước"
    role: "Ai giải quyết trước?"
    tone: "amber"
    summary: "Bước 1: Tranh luận chuyên môn lành mạnh → **để nhóm tự giải quyết** theo Team Charter. Bước 2: Leo thang thành căng thẳng cá nhân → PM **gặp riêng 1-1 kín đáo** tìm nguyên nhân gốc. Bước 3: Đưa các bên ngồi lại phân tích dữ liệu chung (chỉ báo HR khi vi phạm pháp luật/quấy rối/đạo đức!)."
  - keyword: "1. Collaborate / Problem Solve"
    role: "Thắng – Thắng (Win–Win · ƯU TIÊN SỐ 1)"
    tone: "emerald"
    summary: "Đối thoại cởi mở, mang số liệu benchmark thực tế ra phân tích để chọn giải pháp tốt nhất cho dự án. ==Tạo sự đồng thuận và cam kết dài hạn cao nhất==."
  - keyword: "2. Compromise / Reconcile"
    role: "Mỗi bên lùi một bước (Lose–Lose chấp nhận được)"
    tone: "sky"
    summary: "Dung hoà mỗi bên nhượng bộ một phần để đi tiếp khi thời gian không cho phép tìm phương án hoàn hảo 100%."
  - keyword: "3. Smooth · 4. Force · 5. Withdraw"
    role: "Ba chế độ tình thế cần hết sức thận trọng"
    tone: "rose"
    summary: "**Smooth** (xoa dịu điểm chung tạm thời); **Force / Direct** (áp đặt Win–Lose — ==CHỈ dùng khi khẩn cấp cứu nguy an toàn, bảo mật hoặc tuân thủ luật==); **Withdraw / Avoid** (né tránh — tệ nhất, trừ khi tạm nghỉ 30 phút cho hạ hoả cơn giận!)."
```

> [!TIP]
> **PMI-standard response to an underperforming team member:** When a scenario states *"A developer has repeatedly missed deadlines over the past 2 Sprints"*, immediately eliminate options like firing, cutting bonuses, or sending them back to their functional department. The right approach is: ==Schedule a private, respectful, empathetic 1-on-1 conversation to uncover the root cause → provide Training, Coaching / Pair Programming, or adjust task assignments to fit their strengths==.

p09-q1.qEn: A newly formed project team repeatedly experiences members joining meetings 15 minutes late, interrupting each other harshly during design discussions, and failing to agree on message response times. To address this disorganization at its root and build a culture of self-discipline, what should the Project Manager do?
choicesEn: Unilaterally draft a strict disciplinary policy and email it to the team demanding signed compliance.
Report the list of latecomers to the HR Director to deduct from their monthly salaries.
Facilitate a workshop for all team members to discuss and agree on shared Ground Rules and document them in the Team Charter.
Cancel all group meetings and switch entirely to individual email communication.
p09-q1.explainEn: According to Principle #6 (Empowered Culture) and the Lead the Team process, a Team Charter / Ground Rules are most effective when co-created by the ENTIRE TEAM. When members define the rules themselves, they develop intrinsic ownership and hold one another accountable.

p09-q2.qEn: Two lead engineers on the team have been arguing heatedly for two days over whether to adopt a relational database or NoSQL architecture, stalling Sprint work and creating tension in the room. Both options have valid technical pros and cons. As Project Manager, which approach should you take?
choicesEn: Decide on the database you are personally more familiar with to end the argument immediately (Force).
Separate the two engineers onto different workstreams so they no longer have to talk to each other (Withdraw).

Create a private forum and work with both engineers to compare performance benchmarks and non-functional requirements to collaboratively find the optimal solution for the project (Collaborate / Problem Solve).
Escalate the issue to the Project Sponsor and ask the Sponsor to choose the database architecture.
p09-q2.explainEn: This is a critical technical conflict requiring long-term commitment from both engineers. Collaborate / Problem Solve (Win-Win) grounded in objective criteria and empirical benchmark data is always PMI's #1 preferred choice.

p09-q3.qEn: A 7-person software project team has been collaborating seamlessly for 8 months at peak efficiency (Performing). This week, 2 new security specialists are added to build an international payment feature. On the Tuckman ladder, which stage does the team enter, and what should the PM do?
choicesEn: Remain at the Performing stage since the 7 original members form the majority; the PM needs to take no action.
Return to the Forming stage; the PM should facilitate role introductions, clarify objectives, and guide the whole team to review and update the Team Charter.
Move directly to the Adjourning stage for the original team composition.
Isolate the 2 new specialists into an independent sub-team so they do not disrupt the 7-person team.
p09-q3.explainEn: A core rule of the Tuckman model: any change in team composition (adding new members or losing key members) sends the entire team's dynamics back to the Forming stage to rebuild trust and working agreements.

p09-q4.qEn: A normally dedicated QA specialist has suddenly been delivering work late and making basic errors over the past 2 weeks. As a Project Manager with high Emotional Intelligence (EI), what should your FIRST action be?
choicesEn: Publicly call out the specialist's mistakes during the Daily Standup to set an example for the team.
Send a request to the QA Department Head asking to swap in a more capable QA engineer.
Invite the specialist to a private 1-on-1 conversation in a safe setting, listen empathetically to uncover the root cause, and jointly explore solutions or training support.
Reassign all testing tasks to the developers so they cover the work instead.
p09-q4.explainEn: The PMI-standard approach combined with EI (Empathy): always hold a private, informal 1-on-1 conversation first to understand the true root cause (technical blockers, overload, or personal issues) before taking any corrective action; never shame publicly or rush to replace someone.

p09-q5.qEn: At a high-voltage electrical installation site, two construction leads are arguing over whether to cut the main power immediately or finish the final connection first while acrid smoke is already rising from the control cabinet. In this immediate life-threatening moment, which conflict resolution style should the PM apply?
choicesEn: Collaborate / Problem Solve — convene a 60-minute meeting to analyze the wiring diagram.
Force / Direct — issue a decisive order to shut off the power and evacuate the area immediately to protect human safety.
Withdraw / Avoid — leave the site and let the two leads negotiate on their own.
Smooth / Accommodate — start by praising both sides for their sense of responsibility.
p09-q5.explainEn: This is a classic exception on the PMP exam! When facing an emergency threatening life/safety or a serious legal/compliance breach with no time to deliberate, Force / Direct (immediate decisive command) is the only right choice.

p09-q6.qEn: For a globally distributed Virtual Team, relying solely on asynchronous text messaging is sufficient; holding periodic camera-on meetings during overlap hours is an unnecessary waste of time.
p09-q6.explainEn: False! Pure text messaging strips away most non-verbal cues, easily causing cultural misunderstandings and feelings of isolation. Virtual teams strongly need reasonable overlap hours and face-to-face video interactions/virtual team-building to foster trust and psychological safety.

p09-c1.frontEn: What are Tuckman's 5 stages of team development and the matching leadership style for each stage?
p09-c1.backEn:
1. Forming → Directing
2. Storming → Coaching
3. Norming → Supporting
4. Performing → Delegating
5. Adjourning → Recognizing & Transitioning.

p09-c2.frontEn: Who creates the Team Charter (Social Contract / Ground Rules) and why?
p09-c2.backEn: Co-created through discussion and consensus by the ENTIRE PROJECT TEAM at the outset (with the PM facilitating), to build ownership and voluntary compliance.

p09-c3.frontEn: What are Daniel Pink's 3 pillars of sustainable intrinsic motivation for knowledge workers?
p09-c3.backEn: Autonomy (freedom over how to do the work) · Mastery (opportunity to sharpen skills) · Purpose (clear sense of meaning and value delivered).

p09-c4.frontEn: What are the 4 core components of Emotional Intelligence (EI)?
p09-c4.backEn:
1. Self-Awareness
2. Self-Management
3. Social Awareness / Empathy
4. Relationship Management.

p09-c5.frontEn: In conflict resolution questions, when should you choose Collaborate/Problem Solve vs. Force/Direct?
p09-c5.backEn:
• Collaborate (Win-Win): #1 priority for most technical/process conflicts needing a root-cause fix and long-term buy-in.
• Force (Win-Lose): Choose ONLY in emergencies involving life safety, security, or legal compliance!

p09-c6.frontEn: When a team member is slow or lacks a skill, what is the PMI-standard response sequence?
p09-c6.backEn: Hold a private 1-on-1 to listen for the root cause → Provide Training, Coaching, or Mentoring / Pair Programming — NEVER rush to fire or replace them!

P10.titleEn: Scope & Quality: WBS, Controlling Scope Creep & Acceptance Flow
P10.summaryEn: Combine PMBOK 8 Performance Domain #2 Scope with Principle #3 Embed Quality: master the Scope Baseline trio and RTM, separate Scope Creep from Gold Plating, distinguish Manage Quality (QA) vs. Control Quality (QC), and internalize the Deliverable → Verified → Accepted → Close acceptance flow.
P10.mottoEn: 100% Rule in WBS · Zero Gold Plating · QC Before Validate Scope
P10.realWorldTrapEn: A developer with spare time adds an unrequested feature as a 'free surprise for the client' (Gold Plating); bringing a deliverable straight to customer acceptance without internal QC; confusing process audits (QA) with product inspection (QC).
P10.pmiMindsetShiftEn: Deliver EXACTLY AND ONLY what is in the Scope Baseline (the 100% Rule of WBS) — any addition, even if free or informally requested by the customer, must be stopped and routed through Change Control; always complete Control Quality (producing Verified Deliverables) BEFORE conducting Validate Scope with the customer (producing Accepted Deliverables).

steps.headingEn: Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM), and Scope Baseline
steps.bodyEn:
In a **Digital Banking App** project, merely listing ad-hoc tasks chronologically makes it easy to miss critical functional components. In **PMBOK® Guide 8 (`§2.2` — Scope Domain)**, PMI uses 3 core tools to define the boundary between **what is in scope and what is out of scope**:

- **WBS (*Work Breakdown Structure* — Deliverable-oriented decomposition):** A hierarchical breakdown of the project into concrete deliverables (e.g., `1.1 eKYC Identity Module`, `1.2 24/7 Transfer Module`, `1.3 Reconciliation Gateway`). The WBS follows the ==100% Rule==: the sum of child nodes must cover **exactly 100% of the parent scope** — omitting nothing committed and adding no out-of-scope work. The lowest level of the WBS used to estimate time and cost is the **Work Package**.
- **Scope Baseline:** The official trio of **(1) Project Scope Statement** (describing product scope, acceptance criteria, and **Exclusions** explicitly stating what is *out of scope*) + **(2) WBS** + **(3) WBS Dictionary** (detailing technical specifications and quality requirements for each WBS work package).
- **RTM (*Requirements Traceability Matrix*):** A grid linking each requirement from its originating **Business Objective** → **WBS Node** → **Technical Design** → **Test Case**. Whenever you need to verify which business goal a feature serves or whether a corresponding test case exists, check the `RTM` directly.

steps.headingEn: Distinguishing Two Scope Distortion Risks: Scope Creep vs. Gold Plating
steps.bodyEn:
Projects go over budget and behind schedule not only from major changes, but often from a series of small, uncontrolled additions bypassing change control. You must distinguish the origin of these two phenomena:

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Phân biệt hai hiện tượng lệch phạm vi: Scope Creep và Gold Plating"
subtitle: "Dù yêu cầu đến từ khách hàng hay do đội dự án tự thêm vào, việc bỏ qua kiểm soát thay đổi đều sai quy chuẩn"
left:
  badge: "TỪ PHÍA KHÁCH HÀNG / STAKEHOLDER"
  title: "Scope Creep (Phạm vi phình to không kiểm soát)"
  tone: "rose"
  bullets:
    - "Tình huống thực tế: Khách hàng trao đổi riêng với Developer 'Tiện tay thêm giúp anh nút xuất báo cáo ra định dạng biểu đồ động nhé, nhỏ xíu thôi!'."
    - "Bản chất: Phạm vi tăng dần từng phần nhỏ từ yêu cầu bên ngoài mà KHÔNG đánh giá tác động và KHÔNG đi qua CCB (hoặc PO trong Agile)."
    - "Cách xử lý chuẩn PMI: Đối chiếu Project Scope Statement (Exclusions) & RTM, hướng dẫn đưa yêu cầu mới vào quy trình Change Request chính thức."
right:
  badge: "TỪ NỘI BỘ ĐỘI DỰ ÁN"
  title: "Gold Plating (Tự ý thêm tính năng ngoài yêu cầu)"
  tone: "amber"
  bullets:
    - "Tình huống thực tế: Senior Dev thấy còn dư 2 ngày nên tự ý lập trình thêm hiệu ứng chuyển cảnh 3D và bộ lọc giọng nói dù khách hàng không yêu cầu."
    - "Tác hại thực tế: Tiêu tốn thời gian kiểm thử của Tester, phát sinh lỗi mới không cần thiết và tăng gánh nặng bảo trì lâu dài."
    - "Cách xử lý chuẩn PMI: Dừng việc làm thêm ngoài Baseline; nếu ý tưởng thực sự có giá trị, phải lập Change Request trình phê duyệt trước."
```

> [!WARNING]
> **Watch out for the "free, no extra budget needed" trap:** Exam scenarios often say *"The developer insists this extra feature costs nothing and will not delay the schedule"*. Under PMI standards, ==any item outside the Scope Baseline that has not been formally approved is Gold Plating and must not be added unilaterally==.

steps.headingEn: Distinguishing 3 Control Activities: Quality Assurance (QA), Quality Control (QC), and Validate Scope
steps.bodyEn:
From the moment a deliverable is built until the customer signs off on acceptance, it passes through **3 control activities that differ in purpose and owner**:

- **QA (*Manage Quality / Quality Assurance*):** Performed continuously during execution (*Executing*). QA does not directly fix product defects; instead, it **audits work processes** (*Quality Audit*) to verify whether the team follows established standards (such as Peer Code Review and automated CI/CD checks) → Focused on **Defect Prevention**.
- **QC (*Control Quality* — Internal product verification):** The project team / QA testers directly test and measure the deliverable against technical specifications to catch defects (*Inspection / Correctness*). Deliverables passing internal QC become **`Verified Deliverables`**.
- **Validate Scope (*Customer scope acceptance*):** Present `Verified Deliverables` for business demonstration and User Acceptance Testing (*UAT*) with the Customer / Sponsor. Once the customer signs off on acceptance, they officially become **`Accepted Deliverables`** ready for project closure.

```visual
    tone: "rose"
    cause: "Đội dự án đã bỏ qua hoặc thực hiện chưa đầy đủ bước kiểm thử nội bộ (QC / Definition of Done)."
    fix: "Tăng cường bước **Control Quality** nội bộ để đảm bảo sản phẩm đạt chuẩn Verified trước khi mời khách hàng nghiệm thu."
  - symptom: "Dù Tester kiểm tra kỹ, cùng một dạng lỗi bảo mật vẫn lặp đi lặp lại ở mọi module mới"
    badge: "VẤN ĐỀ Ở MANAGE QUALITY (QA)"
    tone: "amber"
    cause: "Quy trình lập trình đang thiếu chuẩn phòng ngừa — chỉ xử lý sửa lỗi ở cuối công đoạn."
    fix: "Thực hiện **Manage Quality** (Quality Audit + Phân tích nguyên nhân gốc rễ 5 Whys / Biểu đồ Ishikawa) để cải tiến lại quy trình."
  - symptom: "Phần mềm vận hành ổn định không có lỗi kỹ thuật (đạt QC), nhưng khách hàng vẫn từ chối nghiệm thu"
    badge: "LỆCH YÊU CẦU / KỲ VỌNG"
    tone: "cyan"
    cause: "Khâu thu thập yêu cầu và thống nhất tiêu chí nghiệm thu ban đầu chưa khớp với nhu cầu nghiệp vụ."
    fix: "Cùng khách hàng rà soát lại **Project Scope Statement & RTM**; nếu cần điều chỉnh tính năng thì thực hiện qua quy trình Change Request."
```

> [!TIP]
> **Quick cheat sheet:** ==QA audits PROCESSES== · ==QC inspects INTERNAL DELIVERABLES to produce Verified Deliverables== · ==Validate Scope obtains CUSTOMER SIGN-OFF to produce Accepted Deliverables==.

p10-q1.qEn: During a progress check, a developer proudly shares that he finished his work package 2 days early and proactively built a 3D chart export feature as a 'free surprise gift for the customer,' even though it is not in the WBS. How should you respond as Project Manager?
choicesEn: Praise the developer's initiative in front of the team and push the 3D feature into the release immediately.

Stop integrating the unrequested feature (Gold Plating), explain the risks of out-of-scope defects and maintenance overhead, and clarify that any value-adding addition must go through formal Change Control.
Add the cost of the 3D feature to the customer's invoice at the end of the month.
Quietly keep the feature in reserve as a backup gift in case the project falls behind schedule later.
p10-q1.explainEn: The internal team unilaterally adding features outside the Scope Baseline—even at no extra cost—is called Gold Plating. PMI strictly prohibits Gold Plating because it introduces defect risk, unbudgeted testing effort, and unapproved maintenance costs. If the idea has real merit, it must be evaluated and submitted via a Change Request.

p10-q2.qEn: The engineering team has just finished installing an automated factory sensor system. A team member suggests inviting the Client's representative tomorrow morning to sign the scope acceptance (Validate Scope) in time for the payment milestone. However, the internal QA team has not yet run the quality verification tests for this work package. What should you do?
choicesEn: Agree to invite the Client to inspect everything together at once to save time for both parties.
Complete Control Quality internally first to confirm the deliverable meets technical specifications (producing Verified Deliverables), and only then conduct Validate Scope with the Client.
Proceed directly to Close Project or Phase and attach the internal test report afterward.
Email the Client asking them to sign a provisional paper acceptance before the physical inspection.
p10-q2.explainEn: The mandatory sequence is Deliverable → Control Quality (producing Verified Deliverable) → Validate Scope (producing Accepted Deliverable). Never shift the burden of finding internal technical defects onto the customer during an acceptance review!

p10-q3.qEn: The Quality Director notices that three consecutive work packages were rejected during testing due to identical configuration mistakes. You want to check whether the project team is following the organization's standard processes and policies and identify process gaps to prevent recurring errors. Which process does this activity belong to?
choicesEn: Control Quality
Validate Scope
Manage Quality / Quality Assurance (via Quality Audits and process analysis)
Control Scope
p10-q3.explainEn: Control Quality focuses on inspecting specific deliverables to find defects; auditing process compliance (Quality Audit) and improving processes to prevent defects at the root belong to Manage Quality (QA — part of the Governance Domain in PMBOK 8).

p10-q4.qEn: While reviewing 120 complex requirements for a digital banking project, the Sponsor asks how you can prove that a minor UI requirement genuinely contributes to an original business objective and is protected by a corresponding test case. Which document should you open?
choicesEn: Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)
Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)
Project Charter
Stakeholder Engagement Plan
p10-q4.explainEn: The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) is a bidirectional grid linking Business Objectives → Detailed Requirements → WBS Nodes / Design → Test Cases, ensuring every requirement has a justified purpose and verified test coverage.

p10-q5.qEn: Your company builds a minimalist note-taking app for students: it has only 3 basic features and lacks advanced cloud sync or voice recognition, yet it runs flawlessly with zero crashes and instant response times. In PMI quality terminology, how is this product described?
choicesEn: Low Quality, High Grade
Low Grade, High Quality (completely acceptable!)
Low Quality, Low Grade
Gold Plated Product
p10-q5.explainEn: Grade reflects the number of technical features/capabilities; Quality reflects the degree to which requirements are met with zero defects. Fewer advanced features paired with rock-solid, defect-free performance is Low Grade + High Quality — completely valid for the target segment!

p10-q6.qEn: The PMI-standard Scope Baseline trio consists of: the Project Charter, the Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM), and the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS).
p10-q6.explainEn: False! This is a very common memorization trap. The exact trio forming the Scope Baseline is: (1) Project Scope Statement + (2) WBS + (3) WBS Dictionary. The Project Charter and RTM are separate project documents and are NOT part of the Scope Baseline.

p10-c1.frontEn: Which exact 3 documents make up the PMI-standard Scope Baseline?
p10-c1.backEn:
1. Project Scope Statement (including scope description, acceptance criteria & Exclusions)
2. WBS (hierarchical decomposition down to Work Packages following the 100% Rule)
3. WBS Dictionary (detailed descriptions of each WBS component).

p10-c2.frontEn: Quickly distinguish Scope Creep from Gold Plating!
p10-c2.backEn:
• Scope Creep: Uncontrolled scope expansion caused by informal requests from the CUSTOMER / external STAKEHOLDERS bypassing the CCB.
• Gold Plating: The INTERNAL team unilaterally adding features outside the Scope Baseline to 'please the client' without change control.

p10-c3.frontEn: Recite the Deliverable state-transition chain from completion through project closure!
p10-c3.backEn: Direct & Manage Work → [Deliverable] → Control Quality (internal QC) → [Verified Deliverable] → Validate Scope (customer sign-off) → [Accepted Deliverable] → Close Project or Phase.

p10-c4.frontEn: What is the core difference between Manage Quality (QA) and Control Quality (QC)?
p10-c4.backEn:
• Manage Quality (QA): PROCESS-focused (process audits, preventing defects at the root — Prevention).
• Control Quality (QC): PRODUCT-focused (technical inspection to find defects in a specific Deliverable — Inspection).

p10-c5.frontEn: Distinguish Quality from Grade on the PMP exam!
p10-c5.backEn:
• Quality: Degree to which requirements are fulfilled with zero defects (Low Quality is ALWAYS A PROBLEM).
• Grade: Rank of technical features/functionality among products with the same use (Low Grade IS ACCEPTABLE if quality is high).

p10-c6.frontEn: When on the exam should you immediately select the Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)?
p10-c6.backEn: Whenever you need to trace a requirement back to its originating Business Case/objective, assess impact when a requirement changes, or verify every requirement has a corresponding Deliverable and Test Case.

P11.titleEn: Schedule & Finance: Critical Path, Reserves & EVM Index Analysis
P11.summaryEn: Master schedule compression on the Critical Path (Crashing vs. Fast-Tracking), resource optimization (Leveling vs. Smoothing), authority boundaries between reserves (Contingency vs. Management Reserve), and rapid EVM interpretation to drive PMI-compliant schedule and cost decisions.
P11.mottoEn: Compress the Critical Path · Respect Reserve Authority · Let EVM Guide Action
P11.realWorldTrapEn: Seeing a schedule delay and forcing the entire team into blanket overtime including non-critical tasks; or running low on funds and dipping into the Management Reserve first before informing the Sponsor later.
P11.pmiMindsetShiftEn: Only compress activities on the Critical Path (weighing cost vs. rework risk between Fast-Tracking and Crashing); the PM only has authority over Contingency Reserve for Known-Unknowns, whereas touching Management Reserve requires submitting a Change Request to the CCB/Sponsor.

steps.headingEn: Earned Value Management (EVM) Through a Concrete Example
steps.bodyEn:
In the **Finance** domain (`PMBOK 8 §2.4`), **EVM (*Earned Value Management*)** integrates scope, schedule, and cost to measure actual project performance. Instead of memorizing isolated formulas (`BAC, PV, EV, AC, CV, SV, CPI, SPI, EAC, TCPI`), you can derive all of them from one quantitative example:

Suppose a project consists of **4 identical software modules delivered over 4 months** (1 module per month). The planned budget per module is **100 million VND** (`$4,000`), so the total planned budget **`BAC` (*Budget at Completion*) = 400 million VND** (`$16,000`).

At the end of **Month 2**, actual measurements record 3 baseline figures:

1. **`PV` (*Planned Value*):** By the end of Month 2, 2 modules were scheduled to be completed → `PV = 200 million VND` (`$8,000`).
2. **`EV` (*Earned Value*):** The engineering team has fully completed **1.5 modules** → the value of work actually accomplished is `EV = 1.5 × 100 = 150 million VND` (`$6,000`).
3. **`AC` (*Actual Cost*):** Actual labor and infrastructure spend disbursed is **`AC = 200 million VND`** (`$8,000`).

From these 3 inputs (`PV = 200M`, `EV = 150M`, `AC = 200M`), the golden rule is ==always put EV first in every subtraction (Variance) and every division (Index)==:

- **Cost Performance (`EV` vs. `AC`):** Cost Variance `CV = EV - AC = 150 - 200 = -50M` (negative = over budget). Cost Performance Index ==CPI = EV / AC = 150 / 200 = 0.75== → every 1 VND spent produces only `0.75` VND of work value (**`< 1.0` means over budget**).
- **Schedule Performance (`EV` vs. `PV`):** Schedule Variance `SV = EV - PV = 150 - 200 = -50M` (negative = behind schedule). Schedule Performance Index ==SPI = EV / PV = 150 / 200 = 0.75== → progress is at 75% of plan (**`< 1.0` means behind schedule**).
- **Forecasting Total Cost at Completion (`EAC` — *Estimate at Completion*):** If the current spending efficiency `CPI = 0.75` continues until project end, total expected cost will be **`EAC = BAC / CPI = 400 / 0.75 ≈ 533 million VND`** (133 million over budget). If the past variance was an **isolated one-time anomaly** and remaining work proceeds at the original planned rate, then `EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = 200 + (400 - 150) = 450 million VND`.
- **Measuring Remaining Pressure (`TCPI` — *To-Complete Performance Index*):** Remaining work value is `BAC - EV = 250M`, while remaining budget is only `BAC - AC = 200M` → **`TCPI = 250 / 200 = 1.25`**. This means to stay within the original 400M cap, every 1 VND spent from now on must generate `1.25` VND of value (`TCPI > 1.0` signals intense budget pressure).

steps.headingEn: Critical Path and Two Schedule Compression Techniques (Crashing vs. Fast-Tracking)
steps.bodyEn:
In **Domain #3 Schedule** (`PMBOK 8 §2.3`), the **Critical Path** is the longest path of dependent activities determining the minimum project duration — activities on this path have **`Total Float = 0`**. Any delay on the Critical Path directly pushes out the project finish date.

When balancing over-allocated resources, distinguish carefully: **Resource Leveling** shifts workloads and ==often extends the Critical Path==; whereas **Resource Smoothing** only adjusts tasks within existing Float and therefore **never alters the Critical Path**. When compressing the schedule on the Critical Path while keeping scope unchanged, the PM applies one of two techniques:

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Hai Kỹ thuật Nén Tiến độ trên Đường găng: Crashing vs Fast-Tracking"
subtitle: "Chỉ áp dụng cho các công việc nằm trên Critical Path — không cắt giảm kiểm thử"
left:
  badge: "BỔ SUNG NGUỒN LỰC · TĂNG CHI PHÍ"
  title: "Crashing (Tăng nguồn lực)"
  tone: "amber"
  bullets:
    - "Bổ sung nhân sự, mua công cụ hỗ trợ hoặc trả phí làm thêm giờ cho các công việc trên Đường găng."
    - "Hệ quả: **Tăng chi phí trực tiếp (Cost)** — chỉ khả thi khi dự án còn dư địa ngân sách (CPI tốt)."
    - "Nguyên tắc lựa chọn: Ưu tiên nén các công việc trên Đường găng có chi phí tăng thêm trên mỗi ngày thấp nhất."
right:
  badge: "CHẠY SONG SONG · TĂNG RỦI RO LÀM LẠI"
  title: "Fast-Tracking (Thực hiện gối đầu)"
  tone: "emerald"
  bullets:
    - "Chuyển các công việc vốn thực hiện tuần tự sang chạy song song một phần (ví dụ: vừa chốt khung API đã lập trình giao diện trước khi đặc tả hoàn tất 100%)."
    - "Chỉ áp dụng được cho **Phụ thuộc tùy ý (Discretionary)**, không áp dụng cho phụ thuộc vật lý bắt buộc."
    - "Hệ quả: **Tăng rủi ro phải làm lại (Rework)** nếu đầu vào thay đổi."
```

> [!WARNING]
> **Budget-constrained exam scenario:** If a question states *"The customer demands cutting 3 weeks off the schedule, but the Sponsor confirms no additional budget will be approved"*, immediately eliminate options that hire extra staff or pay overtime (`Crashing`) — the valid choice is ==reviewing the Critical Path to apply Fast-Tracking while tightly controlling rework risk==.

> [!TIP]
> **Combining Schedule and EVM analysis:** If a question gives **`SPI = 0.84` and `CPI = 1.15`**, the project is **behind schedule yet under budget** → the logical choice to recover time on the Critical Path is ==Crashing (leveraging the budget surplus to add resources and shorten duration)==.

p11-q1.qEn: An embedded hardware development project is 3 weeks behind schedule on the **Critical Path**. Executive leadership insists on keeping the commercial launch date unchanged, but confirms **no extra budget can be allocated** and **no features may be cut**. What should the Project Manager do **BEST**?
choicesEn: Hire 2 temporary QA engineers to shorten the final testing phase.
Review Critical Path activities with discretionary dependencies to perform Fast-Tracking while closely monitoring rework risk.
Transfer staff from another project to work paid weekend overtime (OT).
Cut the integration testing process in half to meet the handover date.
p11-q1.explainEn: When budget is locked ('no extra money') and Scope/Quality cannot be reduced, **Crashing** (hiring staff/paid OT) and cutting testing (violating Quality) are both ruled out. The PMI-standard choice is reviewing the **Critical Path** to apply **Fast-Tracking** on discretionary dependencies while actively managing Rework risk.

p11-q2.qEn: Month 4 performance data shows: `BAC = $500,000`, `PV = $250,000`, `EV = $200,000`, `AC = $250,000`. Which diagnosis **MOST ACCURATELY** reflects the project's current health?
choicesEn: The project is on budget because AC equals PV ($250,000), but behind schedule.
The project is ahead of schedule but severely over budget.
The project is both behind schedule (`SPI = 0.80`) and over budget (`CPI = 0.80`).
The project is under budget (`CPI = 1.25`) but behind schedule (`SPI = 0.80`).
p11-q2.explainEn: Avoid the trap of comparing `AC` directly with `PV`! Every EVM formula uses `EV` as the anchor: `SPI = EV / PV = 200k / 250k = 0.80` (< 1 → behind schedule) and `CPI = EV / AC = 200k / 250k = 0.80` (< 1 → over budget).

p11-q3.qEn: During data center construction, an unexpected new component import tariff is enacted, adding `$45,000` in costs. This risk was **never identified** in the `Risk Register`. How should the Project Manager handle the funding?
choicesEn: Proactively draw `$45,000` from the Management Reserve since it is a project reserve.
Quietly pull unused funds from the Contingency Reserve of another work package to cover the gap.
Assess the overall impact and submit a Change Request to the Sponsor/CCB for approval to use Management Reserve, then update the Cost Baseline.
Require the contractor to absorb the entire unforeseen tariff cost.
p11-q3.explainEn: A completely unidentified event falls under **Unknown-Unknowns** and requires **Management Reserve**. However, Management Reserve sits OUTSIDE the `Cost Baseline` and is not under the PM's unilateral spending authority — the PM must submit a **Change Request** for Sponsor/CCB approval to move those funds into the `Cost Baseline`.

p11-q4.qEn: When a solutions architect is double-booked at 14 hours/day across two parallel workstreams, if the PM must **preserve the project finish date (without extending the Critical Path)**, they should try **Resource Smoothing** first rather than **Resource Leveling**.
p11-q4.explainEn: True! **Resource Smoothing** only shifts activities within their available `Total/Free Float`, leaving the Critical Path and project end date intact; whereas **Resource Leveling** can push back Critical Path activities and therefore often extends the overall schedule.

p11-q5.qEn: Activity **B** sits on a non-critical path with `Total Float = 6 days` and `Free Float = 2 days`. Due to a test environment outage, activity **B** finishes **4 days** late. What is the resulting impact?
choicesEn: The final project completion date is delayed by 4 days.
The Early Start of the immediate successor activity after B is pushed back by 2 days, while the overall project completion date remains UNAFFECTED.
Neither the successor activity nor the project completion date is affected.
Activity B immediately becomes the new Critical Path with negative Total Float (-2 days).
p11-q5.explainEn: Because the `4-day` delay exceeds `Free Float (2 days)`, the immediate successor after B is delayed by `4 - 2 = 2 days`. However, `4 days` is still within `Total Float (6 days)`, so total project slack is not exhausted — the final project completion date remains unchanged!

p11-q6.qEn: Midway through a project, a minor warehouse fire damages a `$20,000` batch of cabling, causing current `CPI` to drop to `0.90`. Upon analysis, the team confirms this was a **one-time isolated accident**, and all cost rates for remaining work align closely with the original estimates. Which `EAC` forecasting formula is most appropriate?
choicesEn: `EAC = BAC / CPI`
`EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)`
`EAC = AC + [(BAC - EV) / (CPI × SPI)]`
`EAC = BAC - CV`
p11-q6.explainEn: When past variance is **atypical / a one-time anomaly** and remaining work is expected to proceed at the originally planned cost rate, the standard formula is `EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)` (actual cost incurred to date plus remaining work valued at the original baseline rate).

p11-c1.frontEn: What is the core trade-off between **Crashing** and **Fast-Tracking** when compressing the Critical Path?
p11-c1.backEn:
• **Crashing** (adding resources/OT): **increases Cost**.
• **Fast-Tracking** (running sequential tasks in parallel on discretionary dependencies): **increases Rework Risk**.
Both only shorten the project when applied to the **Critical Path**.

p11-c2.frontEn: How do **Resource Leveling** and **Resource Smoothing** differ in their impact on the Critical Path?
p11-c2.backEn:
• **Resource Leveling:** resolves resource over-allocation completely, but **often extends the Critical Path**.
• **Resource Smoothing:** adjusts tasks only within available Float, so it **NEVER changes the Critical Path** (though it may not resolve 100% of over-allocation).

p11-c3.frontEn: How does **Contingency Reserve** differ from **Management Reserve** in risk type, `Cost Baseline` placement, and approval authority?
p11-c3.backEn:
• **Contingency Reserve:** for *Known-Unknowns*, **INSIDE the Cost Baseline**, **PM can use directly** when an identified risk occurs.
• **Management Reserve:** for *Unknown-Unknowns*, **OUTSIDE the Cost Baseline** (added on top to form the Project Budget), **requires a Change Request** approved by the Sponsor/CCB.

p11-c4.frontEn: Quickly read EVM signals: when is a project behind schedule, over budget, and when does `TCPI` flash a red alert?
p11-c4.backEn:
• `SPI = EV / PV < 1.0` → **Behind schedule**.
• `CPI = EV / AC < 1.0` → **Over budget**.
• `TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) > 1.0` → Remaining work must be executed at a stricter cost efficiency to stay within `BAC`.

p11-c5.frontEn: When do you use `EAC = BAC / CPI` vs. `EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)`?
p11-c5.backEn:
• `EAC = BAC / CPI`: when current cost variance is **Typical** and expected to continue through project completion.
• `EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)`: when past variance was a **one-time Atypical event**, and remaining work will return to the original planned cost rate.

p11-c6.backEn:
• **Total Float:** the amount of time an activity can be delayed **without delaying the overall project finish date** (`Total Float = 0` on a standard Critical Path).
• **Free Float:** the amount of time an activity can be delayed **without delaying the Early Start of any immediate successor activity**.

P12.titleEn: Risk & Procurement: Distinguishing Risk vs Issue, Response Strategies & Contracts
P12.summaryEn: Clearly distinguish between a Risk (an uncertain future event → Risk Register) and an Issue (an event that has already occurred → Issue Log), master the 10 Threat/Opportunity response strategies along with Residual vs. Secondary Risk, select the right contract type based on scope clarity, and handle Vendor disputes following the ADR hierarchy.
P12.mottoEn: Future is Risk · Present is Issue · Match Contract to Uncertainty · Negotiate First
P12.realWorldTrapEn: An incident has already erupted in Production, yet you still choose 'Update the Risk Register and calculate probability'; or the moment a Vendor delivers defective work, you threaten contract termination and immediate litigation.
P12.pmiMindsetShiftEn: Determine the timeline in the first 3 seconds: if it hasn't happened yet, it's a Risk; if it has already happened (100%), it's an Issue (record in the Issue Log + execute the Contingency Plan or a Workaround); with Vendors, always open the SOW/Contract to verify the terms first, then prioritize direct Negotiation before using ADR.

steps.headingEn: Distinguishing Risk (Future Uncertain Event) and Issue (Current Occurred Event)
steps.bodyEn:
In **Domain #7 Risk** (`PMBOK 8 §2.7`), a common point-losing mistake is failing to accurately identify the **event's timeline** in the question. Consider these two scenarios in a software project:

- **Scenario A:** *"The partner's payment gateway is unstable and **is at risk of** overloading during the weekend promotion!"* → The event **has not happened yet** (probability between `1%` and `99%`). This is a **Risk**. It must be logged in the **`Risk Register`**, assigned to a **`Risk Owner`**, assessed for probability × impact (`P × I`), and prepared with a **`Contingency Plan`**.
- **Scenario B:** *"The partner's payment gateway **went down at 8:00 AM today**, and customers currently cannot check out!"* → The event **has already occurred** (probability `= 100%`). This is no longer a risk—it is an **Issue**. ==Once an event has occurred, it must be logged immediately in the Issue Log==: if a response plan was prepared in advance, activate the `Contingency Plan`; if it is an unforeseen surprise incident, deploy an immediate improvised response called a **`Workaround`**.

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Quy tắc Phân tách Risk và Issue"
subtitle: "Chọn đúng tài liệu ghi nhận (Risk Register vs Issue Log) để xử lý chính xác"
left:
  badge: "TƯƠNG LAI · XÁC SUẤT < 100%"
  title: "Risk (Rủi ro: Đe doạ hoặc Cơ hội)"
  tone: "amber"
  bullets:
    - "Từ khoá nhận diện: *có thể (might/may/could)*, *nguy cơ*, *lo ngại rằng*, *nếu xảy ra thì...*."
    - "Hồ sơ ghi nhận đầu tiên: **Risk Register** (kèm chỉ định Risk Owner)."
    - "Quy trình tiếp theo: Phân tích định tính (Qualitative P×I) → Định lượng (nếu cần) → Lập Risk Response."
right:
  badge: "HIỆN TẠI · ĐÃ XẢY RA = 100%"
  title: "Issue (Sự cố / Vấn đề đang diễn ra)"
  tone: "rose"
  bullets:
    - "Từ khoá nhận diện: *đã nghỉ việc (has resigned)*, *vừa bị khoá*, *nhà thầu vừa báo trễ*, *phát hiện lỗi*."
    - "Hồ sơ ghi nhận đầu tiên: **Issue Log** (gán Issue Owner chịu trách nhiệm xử lý)."
    - "Hành động: Đã có phương án sẵn → chạy **Contingency Plan**; chưa lường trước → lập **Workaround**."
```

steps.headingEn: Ten Risk Response Strategies & Two Post-Response Risk Types
steps.bodyEn:
In PMI standards, the term `Risk` is neutral and encompasses both **Threats** (negative risks) and **Opportunities** (positive risks—for example, earning a major bonus for early completion). Each side has exactly **5 symmetrical strategies**:

```visual
kind: groups
title: "Đối xứng 5 Chiến lược Threat ↔ 5 Chiến lược Opportunity"
subtitle: "Học theo từng cặp gương soi giúp bạn nhớ trọn 10 chiến lược trong 2 phút"
columns: 2
items:
  - icon: "shield"
    title: "5 Chiến lược xử lý Threat (Tiêu cực)"
    badge: "ĐẨY LÙI P HOẶC I"
    tone: "rose"
    bullets:
      - "**Escalate (Báo cấp trên):** Vượt thẩm quyền PM hoặc lan sang dự án khác → bàn giao hẳn lên Program/Sponsor."
      - "**Avoid (Né tránh — đưa P về 0%):** Bỏ tính năng quá mạo hiểm, đổi công nghệ an toàn hoặc lùi lịch né mùa bão."
      - "**Transfer (Chuyển giao):** Mua bảo hiểm, yêu cầu bảo lãnh ngân hàng hoặc thuê khoán bên thứ ba gánh trách nhiệm tài chính."
      - "**Mitigate (Giảm thiểu):** Làm thử POC sớm, thêm máy chủ dự phòng hoặc đào tạo trước để hạ xác suất/thiệt hại."
      - "**Accept (Chấp nhận):** *Active* = để sẵn tiền/thời gian trong Contingency Reserve; *Passive* = ghi sổ theo dõi."
  - icon: "zap"
    title: "5 Chiến lược đón bắt Opportunity (Tích cực)"
    badge: "KHUẾCH ĐẠI P HOẶC I"
    tone: "emerald"
    bullets:
      - "**Escalate:** Cơ hội chiến lược vượt tầm dự án → chuyển lên cấp danh mục đầu tư của tập đoàn khai thác."
      - "**Exploit (Khai thác 100% — đẩy P lên 100%):** Điều ngay kiến trúc sư giỏi nhất vào làm để chắc chắn giành khoản thưởng hoàn thành sớm."
      - "**Share (Chia sẻ):** Lập liên danh (Joint Venture) với công ty đối tác có thế mạnh chuyên biệt để cùng chia lợi ích."
      - "**Enhance (Tăng cường):** Cấp thêm tài nguyên để tăng khả năng về đích sớm (tăng P hoặc I nhưng chưa tới 100%)."
      - "**Accept:** Không tốn thêm tiền đầu tư, nếu cơ hội tự gõ cửa thì vui vẻ đón nhận."
```

After implementing a response measure, do not confuse these two post-response concepts:
- **Residual Risk:** The minor risk that **remains** after precautions have been taken (for example, after setting up a backup server, there is still a 1% risk of fiber-optic cuts across both regions).
- **Secondary Risk:** A **brand-new risk created directly by the response measure itself** (for example, outsourcing a security module to `Transfer` the staffing-shortage risk creates a new risk of source-code intellectual property leakage!).

steps.headingEn: Selecting Procurement Contracts (FFP · CPFF · CPIF · T&M) by Scope Clarity and Cost Risk
steps.bodyEn:
When a project hires an external contractor (*Vendor / Seller*), the **Plan Sourcing Strategy** process (`PMBOK 8 §2.1 & Appendix X4`) requires selecting the contract type based on 2 factors: **how well-defined the scope of work is** and **which party bears the risk of cost overruns**:

| Contract Abbreviation | Characteristics & Software Example | Who Bears Cost-Overrun Risk? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **FFP** *(Firm Fixed Price)* | Scope is **100% crystal clear** (e.g., slicing UI for exactly 12 finalized Figma screens). Hard fixed price of 600M VND—if the vendor falls behind, they absorb the loss! *(Variants: `FPIF` adds an incentive fee for beating schedule/cost; `FP-EPA` adjusts for multi-year inflation).* | ==Seller bears the highest risk== |
| **CPFF** *(Cost Plus Fixed Fee)* | Scope is **unclear, novel R&D** (e.g., experimenting with an AI model for X-ray diagnosis). The buyer reimburses all allowable actual costs plus a fixed profit fee for the vendor. | ==Buyer bears the entire cost-overrun risk== |
| **CPIF** *(Cost Plus Incentive Fee)* | Similar to CPFF, but includes a **reward/penalty sharing ratio** (e.g., 80/20) if the vendor beats or exceeds the target cost. | Buyer still bears the primary risk, though both parties share an incentive to save costs |
| **T&M** *(Time & Materials)* | Urgently hiring 2 Cloud DevOps specialists billed at `$70/hour` when total effort cannot yet be estimated. **Must include a maximum `NTE` (*Not-To-Exceed*) cap and a time limit!** | Shared risk (dangerous for the Buyer if the NTE cap is omitted!) |

> [!WARNING]
> **Contract mismatch trap on the exam:** If the question states *"Project requirements are unclear and change continuously every month"*, never choose **FFP** (because the vendor will pad a massive contingency buffer into the bid or constantly file Change Requests for extra fees!). Choose a flexible contract instead (Agile Multi-tiered / Cost-reimbursable / capped T&M).
